articles.title: Misogyny and sexism of Russell Brand case have not gone away, say TV insiders
articles.summary:
Concerns remain that media industry is still failing to confront troubling behaviour

Even within the culture of casual misogyny and sexism that pervaded the TV world in the mid-noughties,…

blocks.text: Even within the culture of casual misogyny and sexism that pervaded the TV world in the mid-noughties, Naomi Harvey and her colleagues concluded they needed to do something about Russell Brand.
Harvey was one of a team of researchers tasked with finding fans of Big Brother, Channel 4’s reality TV juggernaut, to appear on the discussion show Big Brother’s Big Mouth, hosted by Brand.

They had noticed Brand’s habit of asking a runner, the most junior person on the production, to obtain the phone numbers of female audience members and pass them to him. But something new had just happened.
A distraught audience member had phoned Harvey to complain after being invited for drinks by Brand after the show.

“All I remember is being really taken aback that she was so upset,” Harvey recalled. “We noticed this behaviour of taking women’s numbers, and now it had escalated to the point that we’d had a member of the public phone up the desk upset.
“We felt as the audience team we had a responsibility, so me and my two colleagues reported it up to our next boss.
“We never heard anything again.”
The episode is minor when set against the criminality exposed during Brand’s trial. Yet it is part of a culture that appeared to indulge Brand and fail to confront troubling behaviour.

Brand’s case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him. The TV world is again asking itself whether recent efforts to improve safeguarding will stop similar abuses.
There were several moments during Brand’s trial in which the TV culture that had tolerated his behaviour for so long seemed to be alongside him in the dock.

One of Brand’s accusers explained why she had not come forward with her experience earlier. “The media industry protects its own,” she told the court. Another woman, an ex-MTV employee, said she did not report an incident at the time because she was scared. Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the channel.

Rumours about Brand’s inappropriate behaviour were circulating within the standup comedy circuit before he ever reached TV screens. Even so, serious allegations about Brand didn’t emerge until 2023 after a joint investigation by Channel 4’s Dispatches and the Sunday Times.
England’s strict defamation laws played a part.

“We have these ‘open secrets’ where everybody just knows this thing is true,” said Charlie Moloney, co-author of McNae’s Essential Law for Journalists. “But of course, when you start to imagine how that would go if it were ever cross-examined in a court case, some of these open secrets fall apart under that level of scrutiny.
“Someone says: ‘Alright, well if everybody knows this, can you actually prove that it happened?’ At that point, you’ve got a lot of work to do.”

Red flags were not hard to find, even among Brand’s public utterances. While on BBC Radio 2 in 2008, Brand laughed on air about exposing himself moments earlier to a woman who was working in the same building in Los Angeles.

He also directed sexualised humour at a newsreader during his Radio 2 show, saying he wanted to “unleash hell” on her thighs, and appeared to make light of requests from production staff to apologise. During a 2007 interview with Jimmy Savile, he joked about sending a female assistant to him naked.

blocks.caption: Russell Brand on stage at the 2008 MTV video music awards in Los Angeles. Photograph: Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic.com

blocks.text: Brand eventually left the BBC after “Sachsgate”, when he and Jonathan Ross left obscene messages on the answerphone of actor Andrew Sachs.
The BBC, Channel 4 and Banijay UK, the owner of the production company behind shows including Big Brother’s Big Mouth, all conducted reports into their handling of concerns about Brand.

Banijay’s report found no formal complaints were made about Brand, but complaints made informally – including some about him asking runners to obtain phone numbers of audience members – were “not properly escalated or adequately addressed”.

The BBC apologised after its review found there were people who had concerns about Brand’s behaviour, but believed he “would always get his own way” and stayed silent. The Channel 4 review found a complaint was not escalated to its senior management team. All said they had improved safeguarding and whistleblowing efforts.
Senior figures from the era freely accept the culture needs to change.
“Bad behaviour towards women was tolerated in television for too long,” said Alex Mahon, the former Channel 4 executive who ordered the Brand report.

“People don’t stay silent because they don’t know it’s wrong. They stay silent because they don’t trust what happens if they speak. It’s improving … but more than half of people who experience bullying or harassment in the industry still don’t report it. And in other industries it is still rife. We’re not finished.”

There have been sincere attempts to promote whistleblowing and address the power imbalances in the TV industry that stop complaints being raised. A long-awaited online portal that allows workers across the UK’s creative industries to report harassment and abuse concerns has finally launched.
However, many TV insiders still say the Brand case cannot simply be written off as a problem of a bygone era of lads’ mags and raucous reality TV.

One insider said: “The rule of TV is and will always be: say nothing, don’t rock the boat and take whatever a celeb does without complaint as nothing will ever be done (and you’ll probably be branded a troublemaker and get blackballed).”
Harvey believed there was a greater willingness among broadcasters to listen to staff raising concerns, but worried that the same power imbalances and fear of being seen as a troublemaker persisted.

“A lot of the time, people don’t speak up because they’re worried about losing their jobs,” she said. “But also, they don’t think anything’s going to change because it’s easier to get rid of you, as a freelancer.”

articles.title: EU court says CBD foods need approval for sale before they can be certified organic
articles.summary: The EU's top court says CBD foods cannot be certified organic without approval for sale. The ruling concerns a cannabis compound whose use in food requires authorization, including before organic…

image.caption: The EU's top court ruled that CBD foods need market authorization before they can be certified organic (FILE: June 2024)Image: Monika Skolimowska/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union's top court ruled Thursday that foods containing cannabidiol, or CBD, cannot receive organic certification without first being authorized for sale in the bloc.
The court said an organic label could mislead shoppers into thinking CBD foods had been approved for sale.
What is CBD, and why does it need approval?
CBD is a compound found in cannabis, commonly extracted from hemp — cannabis varieties with low levels of THC. Unlike THC, CBD does not produce a high.
The compound is widely marketed in oils, capsules and gummies as a wellness ingredient, often with claims about sleep, stress or pain relief.

The European Commission classifies CBD as a "novel food" — a food not consumed to a significant degree in the EU before May 15, 1997. Such foods require a safety assessment and authorization before they can legally be marketed.
The court noted that CBD has not yet received that authorization, although it did not say that it was unsafe.
CBD is also found in medical marijuana, but the ruling concerns its use in food rather than medicines.
What does that mean for organic certification?
The court said meeting organic production standards did not remove the need for market authorization.
"Such certification contributes to the promotion of those products and conveys, in the eyes of consumers, a positive image of quality and approval," the court said.
The restriction also covers products intended for export outside the EU.
Medical cannabis: Helpful or overhyped?
The ruling concerns CBD-based or CBD-enriched foods that lack EU market authorization, rather than all cannabis-derived foods.
Some cannabis-derived foods, such as hemp seeds and ordinary hemp seed oil, can legally be sold and certified organic if they meet the relevant standards.
Why did the case reach the court?

France's organic farming regulator, INAO, told certification bodies that CBD-based products and CBD-enriched foods could not be certified organic. It also barred CBD as an ingredient in certified organic foods, while exempting hemp oil not enriched with CBD.
A hemp industry association challenged those restrictions before France's Council of State, which referred the case to the EU court.
The French court must now resolve the dispute in line with the EU court's interpretation.

articles.summary: DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

image.caption: Russian athletes are competing under their national flag and colors at the World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo, ChinaImage: Giorgio Scala/DBM Deepbluemedia/Insidefoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.
Men, muscles, and the pursuit of the ‘perfect body’

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.
Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside the events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."
ITA: Russians among top 10 tested nationalities

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the ten most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said, adding that "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."
Koehler, though, is unconvinced.

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."
The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

blocks.caption: Only 4 of the 16 weightlifters on the Russian world championship team underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing AgencyImage: Giorgio Scala/DBM Deepbluemedia/Insidefoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sochi's enduring legacy

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.
The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

blocks.caption: Russia's state-sponsored doping program came to light in the aftermath of the 2014 Sochi Winter OlympicsImage: Getty Images

blocks.text: WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."
It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."
Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.
"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.
"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."
RUSADA's independence under scrutiny
Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.
Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the head of the agency, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.
Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."
WADA would only confirm to DW that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

articles.title: BT cuts almost 8,000 jobs amid sweeping cost-saving programme
articles.summary: Telecoms group reports £1.1bn pre-tax profit in six months to end of September and share price touches five-year high

blocks.text: BT has cut almost 8,000 jobs from its workforce since the end of March, as it pushes ahead with sweeping cost cuts across the business.

The telecoms group said its workforce had fallen by 7,731 to 90,000, excluding staff in its international business, which is being spun out in a joint venture with the US telecoms company Verizon. It had a workforce, including contractors, of about 130,000 people two years ago.
Most of the cuts have been at BT’s Openreach division, as the buildout of its fibre network slows, as well as through a drive to slash billions in costs by 2030.
The huge cuts helped bolster BT’s pre-tax profit in the year by 12% to £1.1bn in the six months to the end of September.
BT shares, which are listed in London, shot up by as much as 6% in early trading on Thursday, touching a five-year high and ranking it among the best performers across the FTSE 100.

blocks.caption: Most of the job cuts have been at BT’s Openreach division. Photograph: redsnapper/Alamy

blocks.text: Allison Kirkby, who had been a BT board member and became chief executive in February 2024, has overseen a multibillion-pound cost-cutting programme across the business. This year she said BT would raise its savings target from £3bn by 2029 to £3.7bn by 2030.

The group’s headcount is now expected to end the decade at between 75,000 and 80,000, towards the lower end of an estimated range of 75,000 to 90,000 set out in 2023. At that time, it said the introduction of AI across its business could result in the elimination of the equivalent of about 10,000 roles.

Kirkby’s pay and bonus package more than doubled last year to £5.6m, which represented the biggest pay award to a boss of the telecoms company in more than a decade. Shares in BT have risen by more than 70% since she started in her role.

Kirkby has also overseen the £400m takeover of its struggling smaller rival TalkTalk. She said on Thursday she was unable to provide any details on plans for the business as the deal was still under regulatory review.

TalkTalk, which is headquartered in Salford in Greater Manchester, employs about 900 people. The rescue deal secured telecoms supply to 2.5m households and vital public service customers including hospitals and schools.
Virgin Media O2 (VMO2), which had also looked at buying TalkTalk, reacted angrily to the deal at the time, calling it a “stitch-up” that would further boost BT’s dominant position.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The Openreach full-fibre network is seeing record demand, BT told investors. It has been rolled out to 24.1m homes so far. Photograph: Nick Ansell/PA

blocks.text: BT is the biggest broadband provider in the UK with a market share of about 30%, according to estimates by Enders Analysis. Openreach, the broadband network owned by BT, is also TalkTalk’s biggest supplier.
The company told investors on Thursday it had record demand for Openreach’s full-fibre network, so far rolled out to 24.1m homes. It is targeting 25m by the end of the year.
VMO2 announced plans to cut thousands of jobs in an £800m cost-savings drive earlier this week.

articles.title: UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
articles.summary: Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’

blocks.text: The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.

Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.

The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

blocks.caption: Pro-democracy umbrella movement protesters on the streets of Hong Kong in 2014. Photograph: Alex Hofford/EPA

blocks.text: The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly after the US consulate strongly condemned the sentence on Thursday, China warned “relevant parties” to “stop making irresponsible remarks” about Hong Kong judicial cases.
Human rights groups and politicians from across the political spectrum also criticised the sentence.

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director for Amnesty International, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
She said the new conviction “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction”.
Wong has already spent six years in detention and had been due for release in January 2027.

In the most recent Foreign Office report on Hong Kong, published last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that Wong’s case “reinforced concerns about the increasingly broad application of national security legislation”.
Wong’s supporters called on governments around the world to push for his release.

Nathan Law, a Hong Kong activist and friend of Wong’s who was named as a co-conspirator in the case, said: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.”
Law called the sentencing “a farce” which signified that China “is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil”.
When former British colony Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997, it was promised 50 years of “one country two systems”, under which the city would keep some autonomy and freedoms.
The UK considers Beijing to be in violation of that international treaty, after the crackdown on protests in 2019 and 2020, and the sweeping legal reforms that followed.
Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith said Wong had “stood up” for that treaty, which he said China had “subsequently trashed”.
He added: “Despite this, the UK government has done little to nothing about it. The more we give in when China breaks the rules, the worse it gets in the future.”

The Labour MP James Naish said: “Hongkongers in my constituency chose Britain for the freedoms Joshua is jailed for defending – values we should all support. This is not a lenient sentence and the government must show China that Britain will not tolerate it.”

articles.title: Amtrak workers’ union denounces plan to let passengers bring guns on trains: ‘Sheer lunacy’
articles.summary:
New policy would permit passengers to take firearms to their seats in lockboxes on 1,500 trains a day across the US

The Transport Workers Union, which represents 360 onboard service workers…

blocks.text: The Transport Workers Union, which represents 360 onboard service workers at national passenger rail operator Amtrak, has lambasted the planned implementation of a new policy that would permit passengers to bring their guns on its US intercity trains.
The forthcoming protocols will allow people to carry on firearms in personal lock boxes.

“You can’t walk on to a plane with a gun, it has to be checked with your luggage and stowed away,” said John Feltz, International Rail Division director of the Transport Workers Union (TWU), in a statement. “So why allow guns in passenger cars on trains where there are also passengers in confined spaces? This is sheer lunacy.”

The union noted the new policy is now scheduled to begin in January 2027. Amtrak had previously noted it was considering the policy, amid pressure from the Trump administration to ease restrictions on transporting weapons, but had not announced a timeline.

According to the union, gun owners will be able to bring their weapons in cases to an Amtrak station agent, who would add an Amtrak-owned combination lock. Passengers take their weapons onboard and a station agent at the arrival stations would remove the Amtrak lock.
“A case or lock could be defective, or an enraged rider could use brute force to access a weapon. Either scenario will endanger the lives of riders and our members working on trains,” Feltz added.

Currently, Amtrak allows passengers to take guns on a few long distance trains, stored in secure baggage cars. The new policy would permit passengers to take guns to their seats in lockboxes on an additional 1,500 trains a day across the US, said Brian Delucia, staff representative at TWU International, including routes that about 750,000 people travel every day in Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor that includes its busiest services connecting Washington, New York and Boston.
The union called on the federal government to reverse course on the policy, noting many Amtrak stations don’t have Amtrak staff or law enforcement presence to respond if something goes awry.
Amtrak did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

image.caption: British actor and comedian Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London with his wife, Laura Brand, on Thursday. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Breaking

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault linked to allegations dating back more than 20 years. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Judge says actor will receive prison sentence
British comedian and actor Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would receive a prison term when he is sentenced on Monday. He was taken into custody.
A prosecutor said Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator."
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life, but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
A jury of eight men and four women in London's Southwark Crown Court deliberated for more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué standup routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

items: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial
Russell Brand blocked from making money off YouTube

blocks.text: In recent years, he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defence, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

articles.title: A bitter end for Ronaldo - the icon who transformed Portugal
articles.summary: As Cristiano Ronaldo retires from international football, Guillem Balague looks at why and what is next for the Portugal legend.

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.
The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.

The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.

It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.
His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.
A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.

Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.
So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.
Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.
When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.

He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.

The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.

A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.
It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.

Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.

In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.

That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad. He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.

Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.

The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.
In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.
Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.
Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.

The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.
Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.

After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.
At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.
In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.
Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.
And Eder did.

But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.
His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.
When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.
That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.

Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.
No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.

Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.
Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.
After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.
In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.
After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.
Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.
The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.
Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

Judge says actor and comedian faces ‘significant custodial term’ after being convicted of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a woman and…

blocks.text: Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over the course of five years of his showbusiness career.

Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was accused of raping women in a hotel room, in a bar toilet and at his luxury London townhouse. He sexually assaulted women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, including at a radio station and TV studio.

The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.
Brand stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.”
Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court.
He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.

Brand claimed he could not remember some of the incidents and that others had been consensual sexual encounters that had been “reimagined” or “unfavourably reframed” after the publication of sexual misconduct allegations against him in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, and Times and Sunday Times reports.
But Brand closed his eyes, as a jury found him guilty of four offences after eight hours and thirty minutes of deliberations.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the panel of four women and eight men, and told Brand: “You’ve been convicted of a numbers of offences, including one of rape. The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I have to therefore remand you in custody.”
He said Brand would be sentenced on Monday.
Brand held his head high and appeared emotionless as he was led away by the dock officers down to the cells.
Brand’s trial heard victims had been haunted by their encounters with the former presenter and that they had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said they described a similar pattern of behaviour from the comedian that started with compliments, flattery and flirting before a “personality change”. “His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty,” she said.

But Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, denied the TV personality was a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”. He claimed Brand was respectful when women said no and that being “rude or acting like a crazy idiot” during sex is not a crime if there is consent.

In his closing speech on Monday, the barrister also questioned why Brand’s accusers had not screamed, kicked out or slapped Brand when they were raped. “Not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave,” he said.

Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Met police, praised the “extraordinary courage, resilience and determination” of Brand’s victims. In a statement, he said: “Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible.

“Brand used his influence, status and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be.”

He also paid tribute to the “professionalism and determination” of the team of detectives and specialist staff who worked on the high-profile investigation, which attracted widespread international coverage.
“Finally, I would urge anyone who may have been a victim of rape or serious sexual assault to speak to us. You will be listened to, supported and treated with dignity and respect,” he said.

articles.title: ‘It’s kind of a melting pot’: how one US city transformed a highway into a leafy oasis
articles.summary:
The BLVD is home to 250 enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums and a performing arts centre

Passing through the Mojave desert on State Route 14, going by landscapes…

blocks.text: Passing through the Mojave desert on State Route 14, going by landscapes Hollywood uses to represent alien planets, a driver might not expect to find a walkable, tree-lined boulevard.

But there are nine beautiful, leafy blocks on West Lancaster Boulevard, a piece of what used to be Highway 14. They were redeveloped as part of a mixed-use urban streetscape in the city of Lancaster, California in 2010.

The BLVD, as it’s been rebranded, is home to 250 public and private enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums, a performing arts centre and a public library. City Hall is just a block south.

The city invested $11.5m (£8.5m) to transform a busy thoroughfare into an inviting public space. The three lanes in the centre of the former five-lane road were replaced by a series of tree-lined ramblas – Spanish for “avenue” and “watercourse,” because dry stream beds served as streets in early cities.

blocks.caption: A mural on the BLVD. Photograph: Carl Smith

blocks.text: The redesign was planned and funded by the city of redevelopment agency. Within four years of completion, it had generated more than $270m in economic output, attracted $130m in investment, created hundreds of jobs and prompted the building or renovation of hundreds of housing units, according to the city.
The revitalisation has also created more intangible benefits, residents say.. The city centre the feels like a gathering space, they said — somewhere where they can feel like part of a community.

John Elford, the manager of Lancaster public library, was a reference librarian when construction began. Customers were angry about the disruption, and many complained about a major city centre thoroughfare being torn apart.
“Suddenly it was all done, and they had the grand opening,” Elford says. “Everybody loved it and the complaints stopped.”

blocks.caption: John Elford. Photograph: Carl Smith

blocks.text: The more beautiful and walkable space encouraged people to get out of their cars, he says. People who hadn’t visited the library began to wander in. Their questions began to change. Instead of asking for a specific title, visitors wanted to know where the fiction or non-fiction sections could be found. They started spending time in the library, perusing books or reading quietly.

The change has made the library feel more like a community space that all residents can share, Elford says. In the past, encounters with homeless patrons sometimes drove other visitors away from the library. But Elford says people have come to know their unhoused neighbours, and sometimes witness their transformations through contact with the library’s social workers.
“They start to get to know that person without actually introducing themselves to them,” he says.

Property and business owners went into partnership with the city in 2013 to create the BLVD Association, a property-based improvement district — a defined area where businesses work together as caretakers and promoters with funding from city taxes.

In 2016, the association launched an ambassador programme, hiring representatives to walk the BLVD and assist visitors and businesses. Brian Morris Jr has seen occasional problems with begging or break-ins during his six months on the job, but not enough to keep the area from feeling safe and livable, he says.

blocks.caption: Ambassadors Brian Morris Jr (right) and Robert Stocking. Photograph: Carl Smith

blocks.text: Nicole Stevens runs Pretty Little Poppy Marketplace, a business focused on selling wares from local vendors. She has lived in Lancaster since 1993, and has a long perspective on how its “main street” has changed. The reimagining has brought small businesses and families together, she says. “I’ve enjoyed being able to bring my boy down here.”

Alex Arreola, a cashier and marketer at the Sassy Bird restaurant, says he’s become friends with residents and business owners because it’s easy and pleasant to just walk around. “A lot of cities don’t have this walkable spot,” he says. “It’s a big benefit, the best place in Lancaster right now.”

Lancaster opened a museum on the BLVD in 2012 to house exhibits and education highlighting the history, art and culture of California’s Antelope Valley. Kim Calderwood, the museum’s art programme manager, grew up in California City, about 40 miles from Lancaster.

The Burns Pharmacy, which is still open, was the only place on Lancaster Boulevard that she recalls visiting with her family as a child. She was excited by the area’s transformation, from more foliage to all the businesses and restaurants targeting a younger clientele.

It’s a common occurrence for people to discover the museum in the course of rambling on the BLVD, including Lancaster residents. “They’ll say: ‘I was wondering what this place was,’” Calderwood says. “‘I didn’t realise we had a museum here.’”

Nanette Rushing, the owner of Nantiquez Vintage Flair, also works in a museum of sorts. Exhibits are for sale: an Oscar de la Renta dress, rhinestone jewelery, a fringed buckskin mountain suit. She staged estate sales and sold items she collected in stores that belonged to other people before she came to the BLVD 10 years ago.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Nanette Rushing in her vintage shop. Photograph: Carl Smith

blocks.text: “This street dictates a lot of things, from food to music to art,” she says. “It’s kind of a melting pot, and we can always have more of that up here. I’m glad to be a part of it.”

As sunset approached, Lancaster resident Frazier Farrell walked past a farmer’s market on one of the ramblas. A booth for cemetery plots sat between one with dried fruit and nuts and a large display of fresh produce.

The BLVD is a popular place with younger residents, he says. They can drift between bars, the theatre, restaurants or standup comedy. The museum where Calderwood works has an open mic night and figure drawing classes. Farrell has been a student and model. He often encounters friends when he visits the district and has made new ones among the business owners.

Calderwood says the main complaint she hears is about the slow speed limits in the district. “I’m definitely biased towards this sort of city planning,” she says. “It’s just not something that we get out here, or pretty much any other place I’ve lived.”
A version of this article was originally published in Governing.

articles.title: Alex Eala edges Czech foe in thriller, nabs Hong Kong Open quarterfinal spot
articles.summary: World No. 17 Alex Eala completes a second-set comeback against steely Czech teen challenger Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals

blocks.text: POWER. Filipina tennis ace Alex Eala in action at the 2026 Hong Kong Open.
HONG KONG OPEN
World No. 17 Alex Eala completes a second-set comeback against steely Czech teen challenger Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals

MANILA, Philippines – Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala brushed off the threat of an extended match in the clutch, eking out a thrilling 6-4, 7-6(7) straight-setter against Czech rival Tereza Valentova to reach the 2026 Hong Kong Open quarterfinals on Thursday, November 5.
Down 5-3 in the second set after relentless back-and-forth action, Eala ignited the comeback fire with a love game to inch within 5-4, before completing a three-game turnaround to land at a 6-5 lead.
Valentova, however, stopped the bleeding in time to force the tiebreaker, 6-6.

Just as it looked like the 21-year-old Eala had her foe dead in the water with a 5-0 blitz in the race-to-seven finale, Valentova dug herself out with a scorching 6-1 rally of her own to set up yet another nail-biting finish for the Filipina sensation.
After four match points, Eala got the final break she needed on the serve, scoring the last two points to seal the deal and deny a valiant challenge from the world No. 85 Valentova.

“It was really, really tough. I think Tereza played incredibly, and we were able to bring the match to a really high level, and I think that was reflected on the scores,” Eala said after the match. “Really happy with that win, I think I escaped by a little bit.”

With the win, Eala also solved a yearlong puzzle featuring Valentova, as the Czech star swept the Filipina in their two previous meetings: a 6-1, 6-2 demolition in the 2025 Japan Open Round of 32 and a 7-6(6), 6-1 pullaway in the 2026 Qatar Open Round of 64.
“Of course, the previous two meetings [against her] were super difficult, so I knew it was going to be a tough battle,” Eala added. “I just tried to be better than the previous time we met.”
Eala faces another quick turnaround as world No. 81 Antonia Ruzic of Croatia awaits on the other side of the quarterfinal equation on Friday, November 6, around 7:40 pm. – Rappler.com

items: Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa is reportedly being protected by a powerful armed group in Mindanao, according to the Department of the Interior and Local Government, while the National Bureau of Investigation cannot confirm his whereabouts.

Dela Rosa has been out of public view since May due to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant related to his role in the Duterte administration's drug war, which has been linked to thousands of deaths.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Is Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa hiding in Mindanao? Law enforcement agencies, unfortunately, have different answers.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) believes the senator is being protected by a “powerful armed group” in the Southern Philippines. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), meanwhile, says it cannot confirm his whereabouts.
“I cannot tell [if he’s in Mindanao] but we have a strong belief that he is still in the Philippines,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said on Thursday, November 5. “Though that’s still a possibility.”

Dela Rosa has remained out of public view since May, following the issuance of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant against him over his alleged role in the Duterte administration’s bloody drug war.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla previously said he received information that the legislator was being protected by an armed group in Mindanao. He also warned that a forced arrest could cost “10,000” lives, explaining why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.
Remulla did not identify the alleged armed group, but the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) was quick to distance itself from the speculation.

The interior chief also gave Dela Rosa a one-week deadline to surrender, and offered a P50-million bounty for his arrest. After the deadline lapsed, the Philippine National Police (PNP) launched an intensified manhunt operation for their former chief.

“The NBI may soon launch some operations to eliminate the areas that we will identify based on the intelligence reports…With the information we are getting, there is a great chance for his arrest,” Matibag said.
Asked whether the senator would be arrested by Christmas, Matibag replied: “We hope so.”

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued a warrant against Dela Rosa in November last year due to his role in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. He was Duterte’s first police chief who implemented the bloody anti-drug campaign, which human rights organizations said, took the lives of as many as 30,000 people.

The ICC named him a co-perpetrator in the case. It added that those involved “controlled a structure of power” which enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out drug war killings.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.

With Dela Rosa still nowhere to be found, Malacañang has challenged the PNP leadership to ensure his arrest, putting pressure on the police force once led by the senator. Will they heed his call or remain loyal to their ex-PNP chief? – with reports by Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

articles.title: One Nation asks donors at $3,000-a-head Sydney fundraiser to accept ‘non-disclosure agreement’
articles.summary:
Transparency experts raise concerns about plans to use NDA to gag attendees at event featuring Pauline Hanson in lead-up to NSW election

  • Get our

blocks.text: One Nation is attempting to gag donors from ever revealing details of discussions at an invite-only, cocktail-dress fundraiser with the party’s senior leadership team, in a move described as a “worrying precedent” for democracy.
Invitations to the “very special evening” at an undisclosed central Sydney venue next Thursday show donors will be charged $3,000 for a “private and very discrete” four-hour event.

Donors have been told they’ll meeting with Pauline Hanson; One Nation’s national director, James Ashby; federal MP Barnaby Joyce; the federal party’s chief of staff, Chris Taylor; and its New South Wales leader, Mike Newman.

But unlike at other One Nation fundraisers – including a $2,000 invite-only event in Melbourne in September – this time donors have been asked to abide by a “non-disclosure agreement” preventing them from disclosing the identities of any attendees. They are also stopped from sharing the nature of any discussions at the event, which is reportedly set to feature a “cocktail and canapé service throughout the evening as the sun sets” and a live auction.

“Do not disclose information about what occurs at the event, including conversations, activities, photographs, video or other details obtained through attending,” says the agreement, contained in an invitation seen by Guardian Australia.
“Do not provide information, photographs, recordings or comments about the event to journalists, media organisations, bloggers or other publishers.”
The NDA states that these obligations “continue after the event has concluded”.

These type of fundraising dinners are common and frequently organised by Labor and Liberal parties. But senior sources from both major parties involved in running such events say the use of non-disclosure agreements is unprecedented.

Transparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, has been a long-term critic of closed-door fundraising dinners and believes they offer “cash for access”. He said the use of non-disclosure agreements was a worrying new step.
“Charging guests for a political fundraiser and requiring them to keep quiet about it raises serious questions about transparency ahead of an important state election,” Moore said.

“Voters deserve to know whether any political commitments are being made behind closed doors to paying guests. A non-disclosure agreement should never be used to shield political fundraising from public scrutiny.”
Christian Slattery, a senior campaigner at the Australian Democracy Network, said Australians were “rightly suspicious of exclusive cash-for-access events”.
“Slapping an NDA on a political fundraiser sets a worrying precedent. Democracy thrives in the sunlight,” Slattery said.
One Nation has disclosed $5,000 in reportable donations so far in 2026-27, across three donations for a fundraising dinner with Joyce, according to disclosures with the NSW Electoral Commission.
In that time, disclosures indicate the NSW Labor party has raised $286,200 in total reportable donations, while the NSW Liberals have raised $95,900.
after newsletter promotion
The individual threshold for a reportable donation in New South Wales is $1,000.
Major donations drive
A now-defunct webpage containing details of Thursday’s event had stated that registered attendees would receive a text message with its location just an hour before the start time.
In early September, the address of a three-course fundraising lunch with Hanson in Melbourne was leaked to the media, leading to journalists photographing donors as they entered the venue.
Other high-profile fundraisers in the state have been targeted by protesters, leading to clashes with One Nation supporters and a heavy police presence.

One Nation has also required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media or revealing confidential information obtained during the process.

The fundraiser comes amid a major donations drive by the party in NSW, where it was polling at 25% of the first-preference vote, ahead of the Coalition on 24% and behind Labor on 29%, according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in September. Polling conducted internally by Labor suggests One Nation could pick up more than 20 seats in the state’s lower house.
Newman and Joyce hosted several publicly advertised, small-ticket dinners and forums in October, with more events planned in November.
One Nation was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Australians are yet to see the benefits of AI and datacentres – and US midterms show they could be political kryptonite
articles.summary:
Albanese should tread carefully as he struggles to make case for how the new technology will benefit ordinary voters

  • Get our

blocks.text: When will Australia see the benefits of the AI and datacentre boom? So far, all we’ve seen is the possibility of changes to copyright which would hurt Australian creatives, special rules about power and water use, and the threat of mass displacement or replacement of workers, with the trade-off being a mere 10% chance of human extinction.
Now add the Reserve Bank’s assessment this week that datacentres were part of growing “inflationary pressures” when lifting interest rates to an 18-year high.

Warnings about looming negatives have been coming for months, but even the RBA has no idea when to expect the positives. And, as the results of the US midterms show us, datacentres are becoming political kryptonite for voters not sold on the AI boom, meaning the Albanese government should tread carefully.

As Labor mulls its long-awaited plan to attract AI investment, this week’s RBA decision demands politicians better explain what the benefits of this rollout will be, and why it is worth the (hopefully short-term) pain. It also requires the government to consider other inflation responses, beyond the RBA.
The governor, Michele Bullock, warned “some pain now will prevent even worse pain” in the future. But why should ordinary workers endure pain that is not of their own making?

Some of the richest companies in the world are helping heat the economy to such an extent that Bullock flagged it in her opening remarks, just moments after pointing to global oil prices, low productivity and expectations of prolonged inflation.

“Parts of demand have also been stronger than expected. In particular, investment has been much stronger than expected, including due to datacentre-related investment. This has added to inflationary pressures by adding to demand at a time when the domestic economy is already capacity constrained,” Bullock said.
The RBA’s statement of monetary policy highlighted that “AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods” in its second paragraph.
But asked when AI would start having a “positive impact on inflation”, Bullock shrugged “your guess is as good as mine”.
She said “if productivity improves dramatically because of AI” – “if”, not “when” – then we would see faster growth, but also warned it could increase the “neutral interest rate”.
“So if people think that productivity improvements will help to lower inflation and keep interest rates low, that’s not necessarily the case,” Bullock said.
Even the nation’s chief economic wonk is hazy on when the benefits start flowing.

These aren’t nimby arguments against datacentres or luddite concerns about technological growth; there are serious economic questions to be considered here, and social ones already being examined worldwide.
Deloitte Access Economics on Thursday reported Australia’s $1.39tn investment pipeline included 37 datacentres worth $141bn – a 36% increase in a year.

Deloitte director, Sheraan Underwood, said the datacentre boom was “competing directly with housing and infrastructure for workers and materials”, and that Australia had “less room to absorb” the investment surge thanks to high inflation.

Deloitte reported “the economic dividend may take time”, predicting “substantial” construction gains but that the “direct economic payoff” wouldn’t be as big. The technology fit-out is largely imported goods and few workers are needed to actually staff the facilities.
after newsletter promotion

Of course the datacentre boom will support AI takeup, greater automation and productivity, but Deloitte warned: “Construction demand and inflation pressures are arriving now, while the productivity dividend may come much later.”

In the wake of RBA warnings about demand, much media focus has naturally turned to government spending. Press gallery pundits have zeroed in, particularly, on green subsidies and home batteries; the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, blasted a “blowout” from a budgeted $2.3bn to $8.5bn.
That’s $6.2bn more than budgeted. Or, in another way, 4% of the total $141bn datacentre investment.
Or 16% of the growth in datacentre investment in just one year.

Economics and finance, like politics, is a series of choices. If everything is on the table for savings, as Labor has said, shouldn’t we consider the benefits of untrammelled investment in AI factories before we start slashing social programs achieving good?

This week’s datacentre backlash in the United States is instructive. Politico recently reported polling showing half of Americans oppose datacentres near their homes; NBC exit polls found 56% of voters said AI and datacentres were “crucial” or “major” factors in the midterms. Datacentres were also literally on the ballot in dozens of towns, with public votes overwhelmingly won by proposals to restrict construction, according to vote trackers.
The Australian backlash is much smaller, but growing. Community groups are organising and protesting. Labor should not overlook bubbling voter unease.

So what to do instead? Beyond leaving it to the “blunt instrument” of monetary policy for the RBA to smash the economy, there are other options Labor could consider. They are novel, but the times demand novel solutions.

Senator David Pocock has proposed a Senate committee to investigate “alternatives” to monetary policy, suggesting options including “temporary, progressive” changes to income tax or superannuation. Independent economist Saul Eslake has said a small rise in superannuation rates, from even 12 to 13%, would take some money out of workers’ pockets and help curb spending. Pocock, again, suggested taxes on windfall profits and gas exports to take more cash out of the economy.

Of course we need new AI and datacentre investment, particularly as the government looks for a magic bullet to end stagnant productivity. But the government has so far struggled to make the case for how this new technology will benefit ordinary Australians, who are left with a feeling of uncertainty and a hole in their back pocket.

articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war
articles.summary:
Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power

The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt…

blocks.text: The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.

A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
Reuters reported on Monday that Houthi forces were only about 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government.
A burst of government dismissals and appointments reflects military reverses and possibly a perceived need to be more sensitive to the demands of southern Yemenis.

Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided in two, and there is a strong movement built around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeking to revert to that division, or create a more federated country.
The government has become dependent on southern troops to fend off Houthi advances, but these forces insist they will fight only to defend land inside former South Yemen.

Fresh claims were also aired this week that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organisation against their will. The growing criticism of Saudi Arabia from STC officials in the media reflects their confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will have to let the STC operate openly. Not all southern separatists support the STC, an organisation that overreached itself in January, making it easier for the Saudi leadership to defer decisions on the southern question.

Some of the most senior figures in the UN-backed government are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen and the government is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries. Critics say the administration has become a “hotel government”.

Earlier this week, its ruling executive – the presidential leadership council – met for the first time in months in Riyadh, where it addressed the loss of swathes of territory to the Houthis along Yemen’s west coast. Since then, the fighting has moved into the mountains around Taiz.

In an attempt to rebalance the north-south divide in his government, President Rashad al-Alimi sacked the long-serving information minister, Muammar al-Eryani, replacing him with Prof Salem al-Awlaki, previously a minister for the civil service and a spokesperson for the STC from 2017 to 2019. Alimi chose two other southerners as ministers for local administration and the civil service and appointed new leaders for the civil aviation authority, the ports of Aden and the ministry of transport.

blocks.caption: Camels in besieged Taiz, which is the third largest city in Yemen. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters

blocks.text: He also sacked Yusuf al-Sharaji, the military figure responsible for the Taiz front and Abu Bakr al-Jabouli, a brigadier responsible for the Tor al-Baha axis. Widespread accusations had been made about al-Sharaji’s failure to manage operations, resulting in the fall of several areas and districts to the Houthis.
The task of lifting the siege of Taiz and coordinating forces has been handed to Maj Gen Rashad al-Yousfi, a career officer.

Part of the difficulty is the tension between the different forces fighting on the government’s side. It has been claimed that Abu Zara’a, the leader of the Southern Giants, has fallen out with the Homeland Shield Forces, which are funded by Saudi Arabia and affiliated with Abdulrahman al-Lahji.

The Homeland Shield experienced heavy losses, leading al-Lahji to file an official report accusing Abu Zara’a of treason, and warning that the situation in Dhubab, close to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, had become extremely dangerous for the government. Repeated claims that control of the strait had been wrested back from the Houthis were contradicted by the evidence.

articles.title: Europe’s far right has a Trump problem after Republican US midterms wipeout
articles.summary: European far-right leaders quick to distance themselves from US president and stress their own priorities

blocks.text: The historic Republican defeat in the US midterm elections has forcibly reminded Europe’s far-right leaders of their perennial Donald Trump dilemma: they may love his nativist agenda, but the man himself is a toxic electoral liability.

Since his re-election in 2024, European populist leaders such as Marine Le Pen in France and Giorgia Meloni in Italy have carefully calibrated their public postures towards the US president, walking a delicate transatlantic tightrope.

They adore his policies on hard borders, culture wars and anti-globalism. But European voters, even on the far right, detest Trump’s personal volatility, geopolitical unpredictability, unreliability on Europe’s defence, and trade protectionism.

Trump’s territorial threats over Greenland and economic nationalism have proved particular problems: no leader who champions national sovereignty and domestic jobs could back threats to invade the largely self-governing territory of an EU member state or punitive trade tariffs.

The sheer scale of Tuesday’s Republican wipeout has now prompted Europe’s populists to distance themselves yet further while taking away one big lesson: angry, economically squeezed voters topple incumbents.
Across European capitals on Wednesday, far-right politicians were actively insulating themselves from the White House, while dutifully avoiding any personal attacks.

Jordan Bardella, the leader of the National Rally (RN) in France and a possible prime minister if Le Pen wins next year’s presidential ballot, led the charge. Without naming the president who ordered them, Bardella blamed the US attacks on Iran, which he said had carried “very heavy consequences” for world economies.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of Alternative für Deutschland, said Trump had promised his voters “not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy” and that “this broken campaign promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans”.

blocks.caption: ‘Trump failed to live up to expectations,’ said Roberto Vannacci, of the National Future party in Italy.  Photograph: Nicola Marfisi/AGF/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the founder of the insurgent far-right National Future party, also said the result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises. “Trump failed to live up to expectations,” he said.

In Madrid, the Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, dumped all pretence of a Washington connection, brushing off questions about an ideological alliance by saying he was “in Spain, not in Michigan” and cared “quite little about what happens in other places”.

Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group consultancy, said all were acting for domestic advantage, hoping still to benefit from the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos and economic disruption of his presidency”.

For far-right parties in opposition, however, the US midterms offer a clear playbook: mounting public anger over rising prices and unaffordable housing can be channelled into electoral victory. That is clearly the hope of the National Rally in France.

Bardella has repeatedly said purchasing power and the cost of living would be “the absolute priority” of an RN government, with plans to cut VAT on electricity, gas and fuel and allow employers to boost wages without additional payroll charges.

In Spain, Vox is similarly weaponising soaring living costs and plunging housing affordability against the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, in hopes of entering government as partner in a rightwing coalition after elections on 29 November.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, made it clear he was ‘in Spain, not in Michigan’.  Photograph: Joaquin Gomez Sastre/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: For populist leaders already in power in Europe, such as Meloni, that is not good news. The Italian prime minister has already faced several waves of domestic protest in Rome, Milan and elsewhere, some of them violent, over fuel costs and inflation.

Her coalition partner Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League, conceded that the US vote was “influenced above all by the wars, international tensions and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families”.

Opposition MPs were equally quick to connect the dots, noting that Trump had pledged to lower prices and bring back quality jobs, but that never happened. And once in power, far-right leaders who fail to deliver are as vulnerable to voter anger as any others.

Some on the European far right, such Dan Dungaciu of Romania’s AUR, sought to play down Trump’s crushing defeat by arguing that reports of his “political death” were greatly exaggerated, but the broader political lesson may go beyond the populists.

The electoral fortunes of Europe’s far right, whose nationalist leaders will in all probability continue espousing Maga’s ideas while keeping Trump himself at arm’s length, do not depend on the success or failure of the US president at the ballot box.

The underlying grievances driving the rise of European populism – the cost of living, the housing crises, the rural-urban divide, arguments about immigration – are rooted firmly in European domestic conditions, not in American election results.

Some warn the worst consequence of these midterms would be for Europe’s mainstream parties to assume they showed the populist tide was receding. What they actually showed was that voter anger over the cost of living is unforgiving – whoever is in power.

articles.title: 1Sambayan says ‘definitive resolution’ needed in WPS issue
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The 1Sambayan political coalition urged for a resolution grounded in international law amid the continued aggression by China in the West Philippine Sea (WPS). The 1Sambayan…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The 1Sambayan political coalition urged for a resolution grounded in international law amid the continued aggression by China in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).
The 1Sambayan said that the unresolved issues in the WPS should once again be brought before a tribunal constituted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

“This is not an alternative to standing our ground. It is how a country of our size stands. We undid the nine-dash line with a pleading and not a fleet, and that instrument remains in our hands.” it said in a statement.
The 2016 arbitral award declared that China’s nine-dash line, now the 10-dash line, has no legal basis under international law.
The move became a landmark win for the country as it affirmed the Philippines’ 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone.
The coalition said the country should seek a “definitive resolution” that came from Unclos instead of settling for a “quieter week at sea.”
Among it mentioned is the extended continental shelf west of Palawan, whose maritime and seabed claim is being fought over by China, Vietnam, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
It expressed that the issue with the territorial claim in the province cannot be addressed by “diplomacy alone while the seabed beneath remains unassigned.”
“Those overlapping claims belong before the arbitral tribunal, where entitlement is settled by the Convention rather by whichever state keeps the most hulls on station,” it said.
It, moreover, condemned China’s blatant disregard of the 2016 arbitral award, which found that Scarborough Shoal is a traditional fishing ground among Filipino, Chinese, and Vietnamese fishermen.
“That refusal is itself an arbitrable wrong,” it said.
It added, “and the case should be brought with a demand for the damages our fishermen have borne – the lost catch, the lost boats, the lost years of livelihood for which no one has yet answered,”
The coalition further urged for an intensified presence in the Ayungin Shoal and recommended a Philippine Coast Guard sub-station in the area.
“For as long as our presence there is exclusively a naval one, that door stays shut,” it said.
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. previously warned that failing to defend the WPS would lead to scarce maritime resources in the country.
This, as a renewed dispute with Beijing sparked over a joint oil and gas exploration plan in 2018 that ended without a final agreement. /mr
