articles.title: What does Trump's midterm elections loss mean for strained US-India ties?
articles.summary: Donald Trump's electoral setback might give New Delhi and Washington space to reset relations, but there is no guarantee that the US will actually change its approach to India.

image.caption: While the US and India remain engaged in dialogue, the relationship between them has grown tenseImage: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

blocks.text: With the US Democrats scoring a resounding midterm victory and taking control of both chambers of Congress, the Republican administration led by Donald Trump is set for a new level of scrutiny until the end of Trump's term.

Trump is likely to face pushback on his controversial foreign policy, which saw the US alienate most of its allies and get entangled in yet another unpopular war in the Middle East. At the same time, the Trump administration has also taken a slew of less conspicuous but still highly controversial moves on the global stage, including a series of confrontations with India.

The ties between New Delhi and Washington are still strained by a stalled trade agreement, restrictions on immigration, and disagreement over India buying Russian oil and weapons, despite the US granting an oil ban waiver in March 2026 and Trump waving some of the Russia sanctions in October.
And while the new US Congress can choose to pressure Trump over issues such as tariffs and immigration, the president still wields significant authority on foreign policy.
Congress likely to look into Trump's trade restrictions

The immediate test for Trump's India policy is trade. India and the US have yet to formalize the interim framework discussed by Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in February, with the two nations still at odds over market access and other trade commitments.
US top diplomat Marco Rubio in India to renew strained ties
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute of Strategic Studies, expects the new Congress to apply "increased scrutiny of protectionist measures" pushed by the Trump administration.
The US lawmakers could push for "stronger trade oversight and clearer standards for environmental and labor issues," she told DW.
For India, whose largest export market is the US, this could offer some breathing room.
She also emphasized that "the fundamental pillars of the India-US strategic partnership are expected to remain strong" and "the long-term goal of deepening economic ties is likely to continue."
'The president is not rational'

Immigration presents a different challenge. The administration's tightening of H-1B visa rules, including imposing a $100,000 (€88,761) payment for certain new petitions, has alarmed Indian professionals and tech companies that rely on the visa program to secure jobs in the US.
A Democratic majority could increase scrutiny on that issue as well, but would not automatically reverse measures introduced by Trump's executive action.
"Both parties have bigger issues to grapple with," said Rajkrishna Iyer, a California-licensed immigration lawyer. "For the last 25-plus years, Congress has done nothing for immigration," he added.
What defeat in US midterm elections could mean for Trump
Iyer believes that legal immigration itself is not a major priority for voters. Nevertheless, he sees the midterms' result as a message to Trump about his immigration policies.
"A rational president would not spend time imposing further restrictions on legal immigration. But as we know, the president is not rational," Iyer said.
The immigration lawyer believes that new, steep fee for some H-1B applications will be challenged in court.
"Most likely, the new rules will not come into effect. And if they do, federal courts are likely to strike them down because the fees are not reasonable," said Iyer.

While the executive branch of government can raise fees to reflect administrative costs and inflation, Iyer argues that charges of this magnitude could deter people from pursuing legal immigration. "Only Congress can pass such legislation," he said.
US still wants less dependence on Russia

The new balance of power in Washington could also trigger a new geopolitical reshuffle and a change of course on Russia. However, it is unclear if the Democrat-dominated Congress will force any changes in the dispute between New Delhi and Washington over India's purchasing Russian energy. During a congressional vote on Russian sanctions in September, a substantial number of Democrats joined Republican lawmakers to endorse trade restrictions against Moscow.
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

"Regarding Russian oil, the administration is likely to maintain its preference for reducing dependence on Moscow, but it will approach this issue with diplomatic caution to avoid straining relations with New Delhi," D'Souza says.
India angry over US supplying Pakistan with weapons
The war in Iran adds another dimension. Any new escalation could affect energy exports from the Middle East and make India more vulnerable due to its need for high oil imports.
But Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the US and Israel, urges cautions when discussing the future of US policy in the Middle East.
"It may be facile to try and parse these results for their immediate impact on specific areas of foreign policy. Much will depend on how Trump reacts," Sarna told DW.
At the same time, Sarna expects Washington to become "a more contested place," with greater congressional pushback on issues that divide India and the US.
"If that injects some balance and stability and restores institutional linkages it's good for the long-term future of our relationship," he added.

Security cooperation is another stumbling block. New Delhi is still by far the biggest buyer of Russia's arms exports, which irritates Washington. At the same time, India has objected to US supplying weapons to Pakistan, including the $686 million sale of advanced military tech for Pakistan's F-16 jets.

"Washington's military support for Pakistan remains a complex issue. However, ongoing regional adjustments and US concerns about stability in the region will probably prevent any significant policy changes," said D'Souza.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline
Trump could 'double down' on New Delhi policy
The broader question is whether the election produces a more predictable Washington or a more confrontational Donald Trump.
A weakened president could be more inclined to seek compromises at home. But Trump could also respond to congressional resistance by taking a harder line elsewhere.

"We hope the electoral setback will prompt Trump to undertake a more considered review of his earlier actions," Amitabh Mattoo, dean of the School of International Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW.
But he also warns that it too early to assess the implications for India-US relations.

"Rather than moderating his approach, the president could double down and adopt an even harder line towards New Delhi if he comes to believe that Indians, particularly sections of the diaspora, played a role, directly or indirectly, in his party's defeat."
Business as usual for US and India?

Harsh Pant of the Observer Research argues that the US president retains considerable leverage over foreign policy despite the Republican setback, and that the India-US partnership has traditionally enjoyed bipartisan support.
How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?
"I don't think India will be one of those issues" on which the White House and Congress are likely to clash, Pant told DW.
But the experience of the past two years, he argues, reinforces the need for India to reduce its dependence on any single partner.

"The need for diversification of partnerships, the need to be self-reliant in certain critical sectors, the need to have alternative supply chains — all of those issues remain where they are. The US midterms do not really change the calculus," he says.

articles.title: Cardinal Advincula urges prayers amid El Niño's worsening heat impact
articles.summary: In a circular letter released Thursday, Advincula directed all parishes and communities under the Archdiocese of Manila to pray the Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam during Eucharistic celebrations.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 9:33pm
Manila Archbishop Jose Cardinal Advincula has called on the faithful to offer prayers as a very strong El Niño is expected to bring record-breaking heat.

In a circular letter released Thursday, Advincula directed all parishes and communities under the Archdiocese of Manila to pray the Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam during Eucharistic celebrations.
The Oratio Imperata ad Petendam Pluviam will be prayed after the Post-Communion Prayer starting Sunday, November 8, until notice of the lifting of this instruction.
"As we implore the Lord to grant us the gift of rain, let us be reminded of the power of united prayer," Advincula said.
"When we come together as one community of faith, we entrust our needs and concerns to God's loving providence, confident that He hears the prayer of His beloved people," he added.

Advincula also urged priests, catechists, religious educators and those engaging in Christian formation to "take this opportunity to deepen the faithful's understanding of our Christian responsibility to care for creation."
"Let us help our communities recognize that the natural world is not merely a resource to be consumed, but a precious gift entrusted by the Creator to our care and stewardship," he said.

According to PAGASA, the El Niño phenomenon from the latter part of 2026 to the first half of 2027 is expected to be record-breaking in terms of heat, with temperatures across the Philippines expected to rise by 2C.

“Most climate models predict that the ongoing El Niño will persist until the first quarter of 2027, with its peak expected before the end of 2026. And its associated impacts may continue through the first half of 2027,” PAGASA Climate Monitoring and Prediction Section Chief Ana Liza Solis said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Six people dead and seven injured after fire at Brooklyn home
articles.summary:
Hundreds of first responders worked to control the blaze, and a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene

Six people died in a fire that roared through a residential home in New York City…

blocks.text: Six people died in a fire that roared through a residential home in New York City early on Thursday and seven others were injured, including three firefighters, the city’s fire department said.

The major fire was reported in the early hours in Brooklyn and brought more than 200 first responders rushing to attend to the blaze and those trapped by it, in the city borough’s Sunset Park neighborhood.

It took around three hours to bring the blaze under control after it spread throughout the building and to another home, and the cause was being investigated. Flames tore through a two-storey house after the fire ignited on 58th Street between 6th Avenue and 7th Avenue at about 1.40am on Thursday, witnesses and the authorities said.
A lithium-ion battery, or possibly two, turned up at the scene, but it was unknown if that was related to the cause of the fire, the New York fire department (FDNY) said.
However, there has been an increase nationwide of fires sparked by the batteries, which are used in e-bikes, electronic chargers and various household devices.
Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, praised firefighters and first responders when he appeared on television early on Thursday.

“We are currently tracking this fire that claimed the lives of six New Yorkers. It is devastating, and it is a reflection of a number of things. One, I want to always acknowledge the courage of our firefighters, who go in every single day, no matter what the level of danger is, looking to save peoples’ lives,” he said.
Secondly, the mayor said, he wanted to address fire prevention and safety.

“We are investigating what the cause of this fire is, but I can tell you that e-bike fires as a whole have increased to more than 400 fires this year [in New York City]. They are something that can cause people to lose their lives as well as their livelihoods. We are really looking at every avenue, we have to keep them safe,” Mamdani added, as reported by ABC News.
Four people died at the scene of Thursday’s blaze, the FDNY said, and two people with critical injuries were pronounced dead at the hospital. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries.
Three firefighters suffered minor injuries. No names or ages of the victims had been released early on Thursday morning.
The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: ‘Revenge of the nerds’: US midterms deliver a win for science – and a rebuke of Maha
articles.summary:
The wins for Democrats come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure

A political organizations behind a wave of Democratic doctors and scientists winning…

blocks.text: A political organizations behind a wave of Democratic doctors and scientists winning elections up and down the ballot is calling the stunning rebuke of Trumpism the “Stem swing” and “revenge of the nerds”.

The wins come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure, as Democrats spent big on health-related ads and as voters rejected the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement.

“It’s clear from the results: 2026 was a healthcare election,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 3.14 Action, a group that worked to elect Democratic health professionals and scientists across the country. “We’ve heard a lot about affordability. Healthcare affordability is the No 1 piece of that. Our doctors and scientists are certainly well-equipped to lead on those issues.”

Among the history-making lawmakers are Democrats Dr Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Dr Annie Andrews of South Carolina. The last time a Democratic doctor held a seat in the US Senate was in 1969 – the era when Medicare and Medicaid were passed into law. They are far from alone: 3.14 Action is still tallying wins and waiting for results among “hundreds” of obscure state races, some of which are not even reporting results yet.

“The voters’ message is simple and clear: enough,” Dr Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a philanthropic organization dedicated to improving Americans’ health, said in a statement.

“People across America are frustrated by the high cost of living, exhausted trying to make ends meet, and fed up with a ridiculously expensive and complicated healthcare system,” said Besser. “They want leaders who understand how hard it is and will do something to make their lives better.”

Doctors and scientists have long held leadership roles in Congress, but until this election, the overwhelming majority were Republican. Perhaps unsurprisingly, scientists studied this: from 2011 to 2020, 86% of the physician-members of Congress were Republican and three-quarters were from southern states.

The 2026 election turned that on its head. Republicans like Dr Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Senate candidate Dr Roger Marshall – both allies of the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – lost. Races for three more Republican doctors were too close to call. Meanwhile, all incumbent Democratic doctors won their races.

Galvanizing Americans behind science did not come without a cost. Trump and Kennedy brought upheaval to nearly every American scientific institution and corner of American healthcare, from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to Medicaid, the public health program that insures 72 million Americans.

blocks.caption: From left, Congress members Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Andy Harris, Roger Marshall, Ronny Jackson and Michael Burgess at a news conference with the GOP doctors caucus, in Washington DC on 22 July 2021. Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call Inc/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost up to one-third of its staff in the midst of a record-breaking measles outbreak. The National Institutes of Health (NIH), the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research, lost leadership and saw path-breaking research stymied amid disruptions, cancellations and censorship. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) struggled to keep up with a historic outbreak of diarrhea-inducing cyclosporiasis. On election day, New York health authorities announced that a child in the state had died of measles for the first time in 30 years.

Kennedy disrupted and defunded federal work on vaccines to placate a base of zealots, as four in 10 “Maha voters” worried about healthcare prices. He also became a key figure for doctors and scientists to rally against. Before the election, 3.14 Action said that Kennedy was “our No 1 recruitment and fundraising tool – hands down”.

Democrats capitalized on this upheaval. Healthcare was the second-biggest issue in campaign ads, according to the Cook Political Report, with Democrats running more than 158,000 healthcare-related ads versus 61,000 for Republicans. 3.14 Action alone spent $23m on independent ads, most targeting health issues including – as corruption became a defining issue of the race – standing up to pharmaceutical companies and insurers.

High-profile Democratic candidates often spoke about local healthcare challenges. In South Carolina, as a measles outbreak took hold in February, pediatrician Andrews was able to give specific health advice even as federal authorities downplayed the dangers.

“I never in a million years, when I was in medical school, thought that I would be running for the US Senate and also talking about measles nearly every single day,” Andrews told the 19th at the time.

El-Sayed pitched a vision of Medicare for All that would save rural hospitals threatened by the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act. His call and response with the crowd was direct: “Money in your … ” “Pocket!” “Money out of … ” “Politics!” “Medicare for … ” “All!”

In Ohio, where Dr Amy Acton prevailed, her experience as a health director during Covid-19 turned out to be an asset, rather than a liability. In Iowa, Democrat Christina Bohannan, who is not a doctor but a law professor, pledged to spend more on research as rising cancer rates became a bipartisan political issue in the state.

“Americans who believe in science are fired up,” said Polyak. “We’ve flipped at least 10 Republican seats and the final number is the low 30s,. Flipping control of the House in 2026 ran through Democratic doctors and scientists – and we led the charge.”

New Democratic lawmakers face far-reaching challenges when they are sworn in. The most draconian cuts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act go into effect on New Year’s Day 2027. Among the most emblematic are work requirements for Medicaid. All told, cuts are expected to result in 17 million people losing insurance in the next decade.

They will also be faced with enormous insurers and drug companies, which will seek to push back and influence lawmakers as Democrats hammer out consensus on wide-ranging health proposals pitched during the campaign, from a public option to government-backed single-payer healthcare. And public health political organizations are already calling for Kennedy to be removed from office.

“In a lot of ways, this election represented the beginning of the end of RFK Jr’s disastrous leadership,” said Polyak. “It’s clear Americans want something different – they didn’t elect all these Democratic scientists just to oppose Trump. People want to see an alternative agenda, they want to see what Democratic scientists can deliver for them.”

articles.summary: 'If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it,' says Ronaldo

blocks.text: RONALDO. In this file photo from July 2026, Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo looks dejected after the match as Portugal are eliminated from the World Cup.
IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters/Jerome Miron
'If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it,' says Ronaldo

items: Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from the Portugal national team, concluding a 23-year international career during which he made 234 appearances and scored 146 goals.
He captained Portugal to significant victories, including the Euro 2016 and the Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025, and expressed gratitude to his family, teammates, and the Portuguese people.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Cristiano Ronaldo said on Thursday, November 5, he was retiring from the Portugal team, bringing the curtain down on one of the most illustrious international careers in the history of football.
The 41-year-old announced that he would ‘hand back the number 7 shirt’ after the November international break.
Ronaldo captained Portugal to their first major trophy at Euro 2016 and helped them win the 2019 and 2025 Nations Leagues.
“It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made only with the head. They are also made with the heart,” said Ronaldo.
“If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it.”
Ronaldo thanked his family, the Portuguese people, and the teammates, coaches, and staff he worked with over his 23-year career with the national team.
“Portugal will always be a part of me,” he captioned the announcement video.
Ronaldo has made 234 appearances for Portugal and scored 146 goals. He holds the all-time record for international appearances and for international goals.

His final international tournament appearance was at the 2026 World Cup, where he tried to win the one major trophy that has eluded him. Portugal exited in the last 16 with a 1-0 loss to eventual champions and Iberian rivals Spain.
Ronaldo did, however, join Argentina’s Lionel Messi as the only players to feature at six global tournaments, one of a host of international records set by the Al-Nassr forward.

Ronaldo left the Portugal camp at the end of September ahead of their Nations League match against Denmark without permission and did not return. He later cited broken promises from manager Jorge Jesus as the reason for his departure.
Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal’s 2-1 win.
After Ronaldo apologized and said he remained available for international selection, the Portuguese Football Federation suspended the forward for 30 days and fined him €255 ($287.16).

Portugal, who top Nations League Group A4, hosts second-placed Denmark on November 14 in Braga before visiting Wales in their final two group games, which will be Ronaldo’s final chances to add to his international statistics.
The Portuguese Football Federation released a statement after Ronaldo’s retirement announcement, expressing its profound and eternal gratitude for his services.
“More than an exceptional athlete, our captain was an inspiring leader, an example of dedication and the ultimate symbol of the soul of our National Team,” said the statement.
Ronaldo will leave the international stage as Portugal’s most successful player in terms of individual and team honors and has become a cultural reference point for the country around the world.

“I spent my life working to become the best player in the world. Today I realise that my greatest victory was having deserved the honor of representing the best country in the world,” said Ronaldo in his statement. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duterte at ICC: Expert report on 'systemic practice' of EJKs sought for admission
articles.summary: ICC prosecutors seek to include reports of three expert witnesses, one of whom states a “systemic practice” of extrajudicial killings during Rodrigo Duterte"s presidency..
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III and JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 8:35pm

THE HAGUE — In a latest filing to admit prior recorded statements and materials as evidence, International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors seek to include reports of three expert witnesses, one of whom states a “systemic practice” of extrajudicial killings during former President Rodrigo Duterte’s presidency.

In its eleventh Rule 68(3) application, released publicly on November 4, the Office of the Prosecutor stated that the expert reports of P-1162, P-1071, and P-1078 are “relevant, reliable, and probative”, and not prejudicial to Duterte’s rights.

One of the experts, identified in the filing as P-1162, analyzed fatality patterns in anti-drug operations and found that the scale of killings could not plausibly be explained by legitimate self-defense.

His analysis compared the number of suspects killed and wounded, police officers killed, and the number of anti-illegal drug operations. It also compared Philippine figures with national, regional and international data, with particular focus on Bulacan.

Prosecutors said that P-1162 noted that the ratios between suspects and police officers killed “provide a compelling evidentiary basis to conclude that a vast majority of these encounters were staged to mask targeted killings, representing a systemic practice of extrajudicial execution rather than legitimate law enforcement.”
Expert report: Duterte-era police killings “extreme and a statistical outlier”

In his expert report, P-1162 also described police use of deadly force during Duterte’s presidency as “extreme and a statistical outlier,” even when compared with “jurisdictions notorious for violent policing.”
P-1162’s addendum also compares Duterte-era deaths with baseline figures from the presidencies of Benigno Aquino III and Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
The expert found, the filing says, that the number of deaths under Duterte “significantly exceed the number that would be expected having regard to the respective baselines.”
The prosecution is seeking to introduce two datasets compiled by P-1162, materials supplied to him by prosecutors, other sources he relied on, and previous reports he authored.
Two academics called in as expert witnesses
Meanwhile, the prosecutors described P-1071 and P-1078 as “widely published and recognized” academics.

The two experts, also included on the ICC Registry’s List of Experts, have “extensive experience testifying as expert witnesses in litigation,” although their field of expertise and litigation experience are currently unknown in the public document.

The filing states that the joint expert report of P-1071 and P-1078 comprises associated materials, including items “letters of instruction”, as well as other undisclosed items provided for by the prosecution, which have been “directly reviewed, relied upon, and cited by” the two experts. The collection also has other materials collected and disclosed by the prosecution, but not provided to the two expert witnesses.

“The Joint Expert Report and its associated material will assist the Chamber in its determination of the truth,” the filing stated. Prosecutors are also asking the Chamber to allow P-1071 and P-1078 to appear for focused supplementary questioning on discrete parts and topics covered by the report.

The prosecution has requested an undisclosed number of hours, divided “as necessary,” for the supplementary examination of P-1071 and P-1078 to expedite the proceedings and allow time for questioning by Duterte’s defense, the Common Legal Representatives for Victims, and the Chamber.

This filing—the eleventh for Rule 68(3), and the latest to be released publicly—is the fourteenth overall in a series of Rule 68(2)(b) and Rule 68(3) applications made by the Office of the Prosecutor in its bid to shorten the proceedings of what are expected to be lengthy presentations during Duterte’s trial.
The former president will go on trial at the ICC for crimes against humanity on November 30. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Neocolonial belch’: what can Britain learn from backlash to Dutch slavery apology?
articles.summary:
In the Netherlands many felt the move, while welcome, was mishandled and say it opened up a new phase of reckoning

Andy Burnham’s pledge to
articles.byline: Jon Henley and Senay Boztas in Amsterdam

blocks.text: Andy Burnham’s pledge to seek a “structured dialogue” with former colonies to help shape Britain’s first formal state apology for slavery marks the UK’s first tentative step down a path the Netherlands set out on five years ago.

The prime minister’s attempts to initiate a historic shift alongside the royal family – whose customary expressions of “profound personal sorrow”, falling short of an apology, was repeated by King Charles this week – echo a process begun by the Dutch state in 2021.

As London weighs its words, while firmly ruling out any support for reparations, the Dutch experience may provide a preview: in the Netherlands, apologising did not draw a line under the past for everyone, and prompted a political backlash, disillusion among many descendants, and a row over what justice really means.

That is not to say it was not the right thing to do. The apologies were “sensitive, the right words, the right gestures … You could feel the sincerity,” said Linda Nooitmeer, the then chair of the National Institute for the Study of Dutch Slavery and its Legacy (NiNsee).

It was about “restoring the humanity of the ancestors”, because a key historical element had been “the dehumanisation of people of African descent”, she said. “But when it comes to real change, the rights of people of African descent, we have another issue.”

Merchants of the so-called Dutch Golden Age trafficked an estimated 600,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to brutal plantations in Suriname and Curaçao, as well as between 660,000 and 1 million across the Indian Ocean and East Indies.

By the 1770s, slavery-derived wealth generated more than 10% of the GDP of the province of Holland. Even the crown was enriched: Willems III, IV and IV made what equates to €545m (£465m) in modern money from the trade between 1675 and 1770 alone.

The Netherlands was among the last European colonial powers to outlaw the practice, legally abolishing it in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean on 1 July 1863, 30 years after Britain and 15 after France. The actual end – freedom – came in 1873.
Afro-Surinamese and Afro-Caribbean community campaigners started demanding accountability in the 1980s. NiNsee was founded in 2002, and slavery entered the school curriculum in 2006.

The political trigger came in 2020, with the wave of protests that followed George Floyd’s murder in the US. If many had tried to ignore Dutch history, said the activist Patrick Mathurin at the time, “through our activism, we forced them to look”.

blocks.caption: Mark Rutte issuing an apology on behalf of his government for the Netherlands’ historical role in the slave trade in The Hague in December 2022.  Photograph: Peter Dejong/AP

blocks.text: On 1 July 2021, Amsterdam’s mayor, Femke Halsema, broke ranks during the annual Dutch Keti Koti (“breaking the chains”) commemorations marking the anniversary of abolition, delivering a direct apology on behalf of the municipality.

Amsterdam’s involvement, Halsema said, had been “direct, worldwide, large-scale, multifaceted and protracted”, and the city’s immense past wealth and commercial legacy were “indivisible from persistent racism that still festers”.

Amsterdam’s apology was followed by those of Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague, and by the Dutch central bank. The then prime minister, Mark Rutte, who had insisted as late as 2020 that a national apology would only “polarise society”, began to waver.

In December 2022, Rutte delivered a landmark speech at the Dutch National Archives recognising slavery as a “crime against humanity” and admitting the Dutch state had “enabled, encouraged, and profited from slavery” for more than 250 years.

“Today, on behalf of the Dutch government, I apologise for the past actions of the Dutch state: posthumously to all enslaved people worldwide who suffered from those actions, to their daughters and sons, and to all their descendants down to the present day,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Six months later, on 1 July 2023, in Amsterdam’s Oosterpark, King Willem-Alexander also asked forgiveness: “As your king, and as a member of the government, I make this apology myself. And I feel the weight of the words in my heart and my soul.”
Afterwards, however, there was anger among activists, advocacy groups and descendants, who criticised Rutte’s apology in particular as hasty, paternalistic and made without real consultation.

Roy Kaikusi Groenberg, of the Honour and Recovery Foundation, called the prime minister’s declaration a “neocolonial belch”. Caribbean intellectuals pointed out the obvious and painful irony of European politicians dictating the terms and timing of reconciliation.

While the Dutch government explicitly ruled out direct financial reparations to individuals or former colonies, it did back its apology with a €200m fund and an initial commitment towards a National Slavery Museum.

The money was divided between state-led educational and awareness programmes, such as overhauling school curriculums, funding historical research and preserving colonial heritage, and social initiatives and community grants to grassroots groups.

Nooitmeer, who has since set up Deeeni, a grassroots organisation focusing on economic initiatives in the African-origin community, said at the time there was a danger of apologies becoming the “mirrors and crystals of the 21st century”.

Mirrors and crystals, she noted, were the symbolic, empty trinkets with which enslaved people were once bought and sold. “Slavery was an economic system,” she says now. “If you say all this was wrong, when are you ready to talk about the economic side: reparations in the broader sense?”

Community ownership of the whole process “was completely lacking”, she said. While apologies might be made, “as long as the community is excluded from the decision-making process, the old mechanisms of inequality simply remain”.

A key lesson from the Dutch experience, Nooitmeer said, was that people of African descent today need some kind of “agency over what reparations should look like – and when they are considered sufficient”.

The Netherlands also witnessed a conservative political backlash. In 2021, only 31% of the Dutch public said they supported the idea of a national apology for slavery, said Sjoerd van Heck of Ipsos I&O, while 55% opposed it.

The numbers converged somewhat, reaching 38% in favour and 49% opposed in 2022 and, in the aftermath, 40% for versus 46% against, Van Heck said, but added: “It’s clear that the subject remained one that sharply divided the population.”

That was grist to the mill for Geert Wilders, who, like Europe’s other populist far-right leaders, has long ridiculed state apologies for past wrongs and pledged to rewrite school textbooks to emphasise their nation’s achievements. His Freedom party (PVV) won a shock victory in 2023 elections.
The National Slavery Museum, conceived with Surinamese, Caribbean and Dutch community participation and backed by €80m from Amsterdam city hall and the national government, is due to open in 2030.

But for Britain, the Dutch experience suggests that state apologies, while plainly welcome, may prove not so much a neat final settlement with colonial history as the opening of a new and almost certainly contested phase of reckoning.

articles.title: Pioneering Jewish academy opens in Germany
articles.summary: A Jewish academy has opened its doors in Frankfurt. The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country’s leading Jewish umbrella group, set up the project to combat hate and promote dialogue and…

image.caption: The new Jewish Academy of the Central Jews in Germany combines tradition and modernity Image: Michael Probst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The western city of Frankfurt was a very conscious choice of location for the new academy, which is the first of its kind in Germany. Frankfurt has traditionally been a hub of Jewish intellectual life, as well as being one of the most important centers of Jewish life in Germany today, alongside Berlin, Munich and Düsseldorf.

Less than a ten-minute walk from the city's biggest synagogue, the Jewish Academy is also within sight of the historic festival hall building on Frankfurt Trade Fair grounds where the Nazis herded Jewish men in 1938 and deported them to concentration camps.

It was also here that the Central Council of Jews in Germany was founded in 1950; Berlin serves as its headquarters today. Frankfurt is also home to the Central Welfare Board of Jews in Germany (ZWST) and a Jewish museum that opened in 1988.

But most significantly,Jewish thinkers have played a key role in Frankfurt's intellectual and academic history. The city's Jewish community contributed to the establishment of Goethe University in 1914.

Another important legacy is the Jewish Lehrhaus (house of study). Founded in 1920, it quickly gained prominence and is today associated with the philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929). It was closed by the Nazis in 1938. The new academy sees itself in the tradition of Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus.
A place of education and dialogue
Speaking at the opening ceremony (November 2), Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, stressed: "We must combat hatred with education, education and more education."

blocks.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier (second from right) was at the opening ceremony of the Jewish Academy Image: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP

blocks.text: Schuster said the institute was a "milestone” that represented the "Jewish community's determination to call Germany home." At the same time, he emphasized: "Jewish life in Germany is under greater threat than it has been since the crime against humanity that was the Shoah."
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier also underlined the need to reject antisemitism "outright and without reservation." He added that it must also be combated politically.

The federal president said the murder of six million Jews in the Holocaust had also targeted the Jewish world of learning and knowledge. He specifically honored Rosenzweig's legacy: "This place of knowledge and dialogue was a source of hope, something exciting and something new."
A bridge between tradition and modernity, as well as academia and the general public
The Jewish Academy combines traditional features of a 110-year-old turn-of-the-century German villa with a four-story modern structure, bringing together old and new, history and modernity.
"We see ourselves as a place where the past, present and future are all explored in equal measure," Sabena Donath, the institution's director, told DW.
Donath and her co-director, Doron Kiesel, view the academy as "a bridge between academia and the general public" and as "a home for scholars and a home for those who ask questions."

blocks.caption: Doron Kiesel and Sabena Donath are the co-directors of the new institutionImage: Rafael Herlich

blocks.text: Donath said the aim was to put the focus on topics related to the philosophy of religion and ethics, as well as on topical debates concerning contemporary Jewish life.
The program aims to reflect the many facets of Jewish life and the diverse forms of Judaism.
Kiesel told DW: "We want to show how Jews live today and how heterogeneous Jewish life is. And that it is completely wrong to speak of 'the' Jews or 'the' Jewish way of thinking."

Ahead of the opening, the president of the Central Council of Jews also named interfaith dialogue as one of the institution's topics, and in an interview with the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine, Schuster expressed the hope that the academy would bring into the public sphere "Jewish themes besides the topic of antisemitism and Jewish persecution.”

But these issues will also be on the agenda. "We have,” said Kiesel, "a problem in this country that antisemitism is concealed behind numerous topics, but keeps on resurfacing, sometimes more evidently, sometime more subtly.”
Germany's Jews and antisemitism: A complex reality

The project grew out of an initiative from the former head of the Central Council Dieter Graumann, who encouraged the setting up of an educational department in 2012. Its work was shaped by the directors of the new institution.
Security measures push up price tab

A mezuzah — a small capsule containing verses from the Torah intended to serve as a reminder of God's commandments — is affixed to the entrance of the academy. Security measures are also an integral part of this new building.

"It is a bitter reality that Jewish institutions must be guarded," said Donath. The academy is being protected just as Jewish schools and synagogues must be protected. "For us, this is a sad reality of everyday life."

The construction costs of around €40 million ($45 million) — about half of which was covered by the Central Council of Jews and half by the federal and state governments — ended up being significantly higher than calculated at the groundbreaking in 2021, partly due to the structural security measures.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
articles.summary: The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo appeared in the 2026 World Cup at the age of 41Image: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.
"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.
"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world."

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals – making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.
Decision made with 'head and heart'
He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.
"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.
"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it."
He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.
'The greatest of all time'
The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."
"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!"

blocks.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo captained Portugal to the 2016 Euros titleImage: Reuters/C. Platiau

blocks.text: The FPF said it intended to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Training camp walkout

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.
Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career – with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

MANILA, Philippines – World No. 1 pickleball player Anna Leigh Waters makes a quick return to the Philippines.

Following a well-received debut tour in Manila last October, Waters will next grace the legendary Araneta Coliseum on December 9 with a series of world-class exhibitions and other activities, while organizers have also promised musical performances with celebrity guests.

“The moment Anna Leigh Waters stepped onto Philippine soil last October, the clamor from fans and players was electric,” organizers shared in an official statement on Thursday, November 5. “We quickly realized that an ordinary venue simply wouldn’t suffice.

“Moving this showcase to the Smart Araneta Coliseum was an easy decision driven entirely by the overwhelming public demand. We want to ensure that as many fans as possible have the opportunity to witness the world’s greatest pickleball player in action, live.”

blocks.caption: How world No. 1 Anna Leigh Waters balances life and pickleball

blocks.text: General ticket sales for the event presented by wellness brand IAM Worldwide begin on Monday, November 9, following a limited exclusive sale period this Thursday, November 5.

“Pickleball is more than just a game to me. It’s speed, focus, and endurance, all in one. That’s why I am more than willing to support a community that values performance and wellness together,” the 19-year-old American sensation said in a video release.

“Let’s celebrate sports, health, and the power of staying strong together,” added the teenage prodigy, who has been the all-time women’s pickleball pro title record holder since October 2022 at age 15.

Waters has also been the undisputed pickleball pro title record holder since November 2025, after eclipsing doubles partner and men’s world No. 1 Ben Johns, and has since won an unprecedented 200th career title at the 2026 PPA Veolia Chicago Cup last October.

Passionate Filipino fans arrived in droves to meet the global face of pickleball in her last foray on Manila soil, as Waters joined packed crowds in various Taguig and Makati sports apparel stores last October 13 to 15.

Already part of TIME100’s Most Influential People in Sports, the young Waters also gamely shared her life success story to fans and media, and encouraged Filipino players to fully enjoy and embrace the process of the rising sport. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.

image.caption: Under Kim Jong Un's regime, North Korea is one of the most restrictive countries in the worldImage: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: North Korea, responded European Union's draft United Nations resolution on human rights in the country by telling the bloc to "mind its own business," state media reported Thursday.
Pyongyang has long been accused by the UN and human rights advocates of committing human rights violations.
North Korea's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency that the move was a "farce" and a "politically motivated provocation."
It said the resolution is "flagrantly distorting it's human rights policy," claiming that human rights are not "a monopoly of the West."
Referring to the protests in Europe, "Streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence," the North Korean mission said.
"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the non-existent 'human rights issues,'" it added.
South Korea to co-sponsor the resolution
The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.
According to the South Korean Yonhap News Agency, Seoul has decided to co-sponsor the resolution proposed by the EU.
It is the fifth consecutive year that Seoul has done so, following a break from 2019 to 2021 under the liberal Moon Jae-in government.
The draft text is expected to be adopted by the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly later this month, before being submitted to the UN General Assembly for final approval.

articles.title: How communities in Cebu marked Tino’s first anniversary
articles.summary: Through the Padayon Cebu chatroom on Muni, Cebuanos revisit the devastation of Typhoon Tino, share updates on affected communities, and call for lasting solutions a year after

items: A year after Typhoon Tino, residents in Cebu continue to face flooding, unsafe living conditions, and trauma from the disaster, with many still lacking safe, permanent relocation.
Discussions among survivors highlighted ongoing concerns about flood-control accountability and the need for urgent flood-management measures, which remain largely unimplemented.

Community dialogues and activities around the anniversary emphasized the importance of transparency in flood-control spending and the necessity for comprehensive disaster rehabilitation that goes beyond just housing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – A year after Typhoon Tino devastated communities across Cebu, residents are still grappling with flooding, unsafe living conditions, and questions over flood-control efforts.

These concerns took center stage in the Padayon Cebu chat room on Muni in the Rappler app, where survivors shared stories, discussed conditions in affected communities, and highlighted activities that marked the first anniversary of Typhoon Tino on Wednesday, November 4.

Leading up to the anniversary, Cebuanos in the chat room initiated a discussion titled “Isang taon matapos ang Tino, kamusta na ang Cebu?” (How is Cebu a year after Typhoon Tino?). They reflected on the devastation of the disaster, and discussed the challenges that affected communities continue to face a year later.

Cebu-based Mover Jerome Valdez shared the story of Alma Quingco, 46, from Barangay Maslog, Danao City, who was on duty at the University of the Philippines Cebu when Tino struck. When she returned home, floodwaters had made their house inaccessible, and many of their belongings had been swept away.

“Despite the help, the experience left a lasting impact. Alma shared that there are still fears and trauma associated with what happened. Even now, the memory of how quickly the floodwaters rose remains with her,” Valdez shared in the chat room.

The discussion also brought attention to villages in Tambisan, where severe flooding continues even during ordinary rainfall, and families who remain without safe, permanent relocation a year after their homes were destroyed.

Violy Musngi of La Paloma Village, during Rappler’s #MoveCebu roadshow in October, recalled how residents were caught off guard by Typhoon Tino, with floodwaters reaching waist-deep levels in her area and rising above head level in Tambisan.

“We were surprised by the waist-deep flooding, which persisted even after Typhoon Tino. Residents in Tambisan are also suffering from leptospirosis. After Tino, there’s flooding after flooding. Even light rains now cause flooding almost immediately,” Musngi said during the forum.
Reymarr Hijara of the Movement for a Livable Cebu (MLC) also joined the online discussion. MLC is a civic group in Cebu, advocating for safer and more sustainable flood management.

In November 2025, they proposed a petition for urgent flood-management measures, including the creation of a Cebu Floodwater Management Office, relocation of families from high-risk areas, protection of watersheds, and a review of flood-control structures. The group also called for no-build zones in areas inundated during Tino.
But even a year later, according to Hijara, implementing the six proposed flood-management actions remained largely unfinished or unverified a year after Tino.

The most concrete development, he said, was MLC’s invitation to join the Provincial Flood Control and Drainage Task Force, created under Executive Order 74 after the November 2025 flooding. However, Hijara stressed that the task force’s formation and MLC’s participation did not amount to implementation of the group’s proposed measures.
“A task force is not yet implementation,” Hijara said in the chat room.

The discussions in Padayon Cebu also highlighted two activities around the November 4 anniversary: a multi-stakeholder dialogue on flood-control accountability and a sustainability walk through downtown Cebu.

To examine urban vulnerabilities, University of the Philippines (UP) Cebu’s College of Communication, Art, and Design (CCAD), together with participants from the University of the Philippines Open University and Japan’s Meiji University, held a walk through downtown Cebu.

The guided walk passed through areas including San Nicolas, Pasil, Taboan, Carbon Market, Plaza Independencia, and Colon, examining Cebu’s built environment, public spaces, transportation systems, and cultural heritage.

According to an announcement by UP Cebu’s CCAD, Tino’s severe flooding served as a point of reflection as participants considered how cities can adapt to flooding and extreme heat while preserving their cultural identity.
The walk also drew comparisons between climate adaptation approaches in the Philippines and Japan, including lessons Cebu could apply to building safer and more livable communities.
Aside from a community walk, various groups also organized a dialogue to discuss the pressing concerns among survivors.

The dialogue titled, “Kahinumdom pa mo namo? (Do you still remember us?) A Multi-Stakeholder Dialogue on Flood Control Accountability and the Continuing Concerns on Typhoon Tino Survivors,” was organized by Sugbuanong Pakigbisog Kontra Kurapsyon (SuPaKK) in collaboration with partner organizations.

During the dialogue, John Roy Rigodon of the Sectoral Transparency Alliance on Natural Resource Governance (STANCe) shared findings from visits to communities along major rivers in Cebu, including the Kinalawan River in Toledo City and the Cotcot River in Liloan and Compostela, where he examined the situation of residents living in flood-prone areas a year after Tino.
According to Rigodon, the communities continue to face concerns over their safety when typhoons hit. This includes being at risk to flooding and lack of safe and permanent relocation.
“Will they be safe in the next typhoon?” he asked, pointing to relocation as a major concern among residents.

The dialogue also raised questions about flood-control spending. Organizers cited P17.4 billion in major river flood-control projects from 2016 to 2025, including P11.1 billion for the Butuanon River, and called for transparency and accountability. These figures were also reported in a SunStar Cebu investigation on how Tino’s floods exposed how flood control projects failed in Cebu.

Moreover, Norika Ishikawa of the Cebu Anti-Corruption Coalition and Center for Emergency Aid, Rehabilitation and Development Inc.(CONCERN) questioned how the government would lead rehabilitation efforts for Tino-affected communities amid reported cuts to disaster rehabilitation and housing funds for 2027.
She said recovery must go beyond providing houses, calling for safe and affordable housing with access to livelihoods, utilities, roads, hospitals, and schools.
“Disaster rehabilitation is not an expense. Building back better is a public investment,” Ishikawa said.

Ishikawa said the next steps identified during the dialogue include formulating a relocation agenda with Tino-affected informal settler families and mobilizing for an accountability action on November 30.
“Nakakalungkot ang sharing, nakakagalit ang inaction, but hopeful pa rin (The sharing is saddening, the inaction is infuriating, but there is still hope),” she said.

Typhoon Tino caused widespread devastation in Cebu, affecting nearly 2 million people, displacing over 636,000, and resulting in 96 confirmed deaths with many still missing. It also damaged approximately 262,000 homes (over 24,000 totally destroyed), leaving affected communities struggling to recover a year later.
A year after Tino, affected communities still continue to call for safe relocation, transparent flood-control spending, and rehabilitation that addresses their long-term needs. – Rappler.com

articles.title: How elderly ‘unsung heroes’ powered Lula’s historic fightback in Brazil
articles.summary:
Older voters praised for helping tip balance in leftwing president’s favour against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff

It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.

But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
Soares clung to the banister as, step by step, she climbed two flights of stairs to the polling booth under the watchful eye of her granddaughter’s husband, Marcio Marques.
Inside, the frail but jaunty centenarian keyed the number “13” – representing Bolsonaro’s leftwing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – into an electronic voting machine and pressed confirm.
“I like Lula. I really do!” enthused Soares, a retired bank employee who has lived in Rio de Janeiro most of her life.

blocks.caption: Soares, with her granddaughter Poliana Soares Jordão, said she didn’t like the Bolsonaros, ‘so the efficient thing to to do was to go out and vote’. Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I don’t like Bolsonaro or his father. So the efficient thing to do was go out and vote,” Soares added, as her grandsons, Tito and Ravi, played on the balcony around her surrounded by pot plants and books.
Soares is one of more than 1 million elderly people who, having missed the election’s 4 October first round – which Lula lost – decided to vote in the second.

Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round loser bounced back, but Lula did just that. And after Lula’s shock revival, elderly voters have been hailed as the election’s unsung heroes – including by Lula himself.

At his 81st birthday party last week, the leftist veteran shed tears while describing his gratitude to the elderly people who helped him clinch a historic fourth term while clutching walking frames and sticks.

“I honestly think it was the most powerful and human image I’ve ever seen during an election,” Lula said of viral pictures showing voters in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried into polling centres by relatives or carers, some in stretchers or wheelchairs.

In north-east Brazil, where Lula was born into rural poverty in the 1940s, a 114-year-old retiree called Josefa Pereira da Conceição went to vote wearing a red T-shirt emblazoned with Lula’s face and the slogan “Strength of the people”.
Election experts are still crunching the numbers to fully understand how Lula pulled off his unprecedented fightback, finding 10.3m extra votes between the first and second rounds.

Explanations include a sharp increase in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote; an extraordinary digital mobilisation involving a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11m members in less than a month; and a student-led street rebellion in which millions of citizens protested across Brazil.

Some believe elderly people were also crucial, noting how 1.4 million of the 3 million extra voters who took part in the second round after skipping the first were over 70. Pre-election polls suggested such voters were more inclined to vote for Lula.

blocks.caption: Lula wipes away tears as he thanks supporters during an event to celebrate his 81st birthday on 27 October.  Photograph: Eraldo Peres/AP

blocks.text: Speaking at Lula’s victory celebration, the former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph which sent a message to the democratic world. “It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” Tebet declared, claiming: “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”

The political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said there was concrete evidence of higher turnout among older voters in the runoff, particularly those aged 60 to 79. Voting is only mandatory in Brazil for those aged 18 to 69.

“The images [of elderly people voting] aren’t misleading: they reveal a phenomenon that isn’t just an isolated case. It’s not some made-up story or a staged example. It really happened – and it was a movement you can measure statistically,” Toledo said of the images suggesting an unusually large number of older voters.

That said, Toledo believed the swing to Lula was explained mostly by fear, not age. Voting data suggested many people who backed Lula in the runoff had previously voted for Bolsonaro’s rightwing adversaries, hoping to protest against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), which has governed for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.

blocks.caption: Lea Zorzella, 90, left her hospital in São Paulo to vote in the runoff election. Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/Reuters

blocks.text: In the runoff, faced with a straight choice between Lula, a familiar and predictable figure even for detractors, and Bolsonaro, who represented a leap into the unknown, many preferred the former.

“A protest vote in the first round [became] a safety vote or a lower-risk vote in the second – even if it wasn’t a happy vote,” said Toledo, who believed Bolsonaro alienated many voters with his “arrogant” behaviour after winning the first round.

Particularly damaging was the rightwinger’s authoritarian-sounding vow to “re-democratise” the already democratic country – something Toledo suspected stoked fears that Bolsonaro aspired to be “the emperor of Brazil”.

blocks.caption: An elderly voter at a polling station in Porto Alegre on 25 October. Photograph: Diego Vara/Reuters

blocks.text: Even before those remarks, Soares fretted over the direction Brazil might take under Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

“His father wanted to stage a coup … and stay on as president, just like Getúlio [Vargas did in 1937],” recalled the great-grandmother, who was 12 at the time and lived through the subsequent eight years of dictatorial rule.
Marques, a 51-year-old food entrepreneur, said his grandmother-in-law was also critical of how Jair Bolsonaro undermined vaccination efforts during the Covid pandemic, when 700,000 Brazilians died.

“She’s got three great-grandchildren … and she understands she’s nearing the end of her life. But she’s worried about the country, about her family and about future generations,” said Marques, becoming visibly emotional as he recalled watching Soares exercise her democratic right, perhaps for the last time.

“It was so moving to see her strength and desire [to vote] … We felt she had an intuition, or something telling her she needed to be part of this … She doesn’t know if she’ll get another chance,” added Marques, whose 85-year-old father, Helço Muniz, also voted Lula – in his case for the first time.

Sitting in her armchair overlooking Rio’s Guanabara Bay, five days after the election, Soares voiced excitement that Lula would soon start his fourth and final term. “I’ve been fond of him ever since he was poor,” she said of the lathe operator turned president, who first took office as president in 2003. “He was poor and he became rich, but he carried on being a simple man.”
Occasionally, Soares’s memory betrayed her and she needed reminding that Lula had pulled off one of modern history’s greatest democratic comebacks. “But that’s wonderful!” she beamed.
Reminded of Lula’s feat, Soares predicted Bolsonaro would flee abroad.
“He’s already gone!” her granddaughter, Poliana Soares Jordão, 46, told her. “His dad’s in prison and he’s fled.”

Soares, who has lived through four coups, 16 presidential elections and four Lula wins, was not surprised. “He must have gone to the US, then,” the centenarian guessed, correctly. “He’d been getting ready for that for a while, hadn’t he?”

articles.title: Family of injured Wainwright soldier holds bedside vigil in burn unit
articles.summary: Pte. Liam Ramage, 27, of Red Deer, Alta., was one of dozens of service members hurt in an out-of-control grass fire at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17.

blocks.text: Family of soldier severely burned at CFB Wainwright describes his ordeal
The mother of a soldier fighting to recover from severe burns he sustained in last month's CFB Wainwright fire says she worries not only about his physical injuries, but also his mental health.
Pte. Liam Ramage, 27, of Red Deer, Alta., was one of dozens of service members hurt in an out-of-control grass fire on the central Alberta military base on Oct. 17. Four died.
Roughly 40 per cent of Liam’s body was affected, mostly third- and fourth-degree burns, mainly to his face, neck and throat, according to his mother Cheryl Ramage.
“Some to his arms, really bad to his hands, the upper and the palms," she told CBC News in an interview this week. "Some of his legs, … some to his back and some to the top of his feet.
"They’re doing skin grafts to the majority. His eyelids even have skin grafts on them, so he can’t open his eyes.”
Cheryl Ramage, a nurse, said Liam's family is taking it day by day, knowing his recovery could take years. (Peter Evans/CBC)
Cheryl and Liam’s wife Marisa have been constants at his bedside at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton. He can barely move, speak or see.
“Being locked in your own mind is a form of torture right?” said Cheryl, who’s a nurse. “His mental health is going to have to be addressed right away.”

items: Alberta government hosts remembrance ceremony as country mourns CFB Wainwright victims
Sask. soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire remembered as funny, passionate at military funeral
In wake of Wainwright tragedy, this year's Silver Cross Mother has a message for grieving families

blocks.text: She describes the days since the fire as devastating.
Being a nurse can sometimes help her compartmentalize her feelings, but it doesn’t shield her from them, Cheryl said.

“I can kind of turn clinical. When I go into his room, especially if I’m with somebody else, I can be like, ‘This is what this line’s doing and that’s what this dressing is for.’ I can kind of remove myself from it, if that makes sense — I can just talk about the injuries, not looking at it like it’s my son. But if I’m there by myself or go home by myself, I’m a disaster."
‘Identified him by his toes’

Marisa said she first learned something might be wrong in a text from her father alerting her to the situation in Wainwright on the day of the fire. The last time she had heard from Liam was a text earlier in the day.

Cheryl’s other son Rowan, who was also training at CFB Wainwright, texted his mother to let her know he was OK. But she did not hear back from Liam. She went to Liam and Marisa’s house in Edmonton to wait for word.
Hours later, at around 3 a.m. local time the next day, warrant officers knocked on the door and gave them the terrible news — “a mother’s worst nightmare,” Cheryl said.
A photo of Marisa (left) and Liam (right) on March 31, 2024. Liam joined the military in March 2024 and went to basic training the following month. (Supplied by Marisa Ramage)
“I don’t think I stopped shaking for the entire amount of time that they were there,” Marisa said.
The pair rushed to the hospital.
“We couldn’t recognize his face,” Cheryl said. “He was completely covered in dressings and so swollen. He was not recognizable. We identified him by his toes.”
‘It’s so unpredictable’

Liam is fighting pneumonia. He has had three surgeries and three strokes, which paralyzed the left side of his body, though he’s showing some toe, hip and leg movement. He has necrosis — the death of body tissue — on several fingers, his ears and nose.
He can now breathe on his own, though he is placed on a ventilator at night to give his lungs a break. Thanks to a special device, he has been able to speak a few words in recent days.
“He mouthed my name when I was in there with my dad and that was shocking for me,” Marisa said. “I did have a really good cry after.”
Marisa and Liam started dating in 2020 and married in 2023. (Supplied by Marisa Ramage)
Both women say it’s hard to imagine what life will look like for Liam, an outgoing, active man who loves music, cooking and playing hockey.
“It is so unpredictable,” Cheryl said. “He’s got a stroke — is he going to be able to walk again? He’s got skin grafts — does he have to learn how to walk again? Is he going to lose his fingers?
“We really try to take it day to day. … We do know it’s going to be months and months and months — if not years — of recovery. But what that recovery looks like? We just can’t tell at this point.”
She worries about Liam's mental health; the deadly fire still haunts him.
“He does say he remembers it," Cheryl said. "He does say that he thinks about it.
"I can’t imagine the torture of going through that, not being able to open your eyes or move or talk.”
A radio has been placed by Liam’s bedside to distract him, playing classic rock and NHL games with his favourite team, the Montreal Canadiens.
“A lot of us talking to him is reminding him that he’s safe and he’s at the hospital ... and that he is OK,” Marisa said.
Military career
The military was always a passion for her son, Cheryl said.
“Liam tried a few other things first, but the military was always what he wanted to do.”
A sign for Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright, on Oct. 18, 2026, the day after a serious incident that resulted in a fire caused deaths and injuries. (Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters)
He enlisted in March 2024 and completed a tour in Latvia. He was training in Wainwright to prepare for a second Latvia tour.
As a military mother, Cheryl said she knows the risks that soldiers face but never expected something like this.
“I never dreamt something would be two hours from home.”
Military, community support
Both women said the support from family, friends and the wider community has given them strength.
Their priority now is Liam and his recovery, not the fire or the military’s response. Three investigations are underway.
“That was a freak accident,” Marisa said. “They couldn’t have predicted that that would happen. And the military has been supportive of everything.
"We’ll have questions later but we are definitely focused on Liam.”

“Nothing [about] what started the fire will change where we’re at,” Cheryl said. “I have no interest in that at this moment. … They don’t stop war because it’s windy or anything like that. They have to prepare in all conditions.
“Do I place blame? Am I angry right now? No. I wish it wouldn’t have happened.”
Marisa and Cheryl say this Remembrance Day has new meaning for them.
“Hold your family a little closer,” said Marisa. “You never know what could happen. Honestly. Hold them close.”
“I didn’t hope that this would happen to my son,” said Cheryl. “I wish it hadn’t. But I’m proud for him.”

articles.title: Bomb threats force planes into emergency landings at several European airports
articles.summary: Bomb threats forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe on ‌Thursday morning, the latest in a series of threats targeting flights in Europe.

image.caption: An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat on Thursday. (Gonzalo Fuentes/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Bomb threats forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe on ‌Thursday morning, the latest in a series of threats targeting flights in Europe.
No incendiary devices found after security checks carried out in several locations

Four airplanes heading to Prague received ‌bomb threats on Thursday ​and police were preparing ​for their landing, Czech police ​said on ⁠X, ⁠adding ‌they assessed the credibility of the threats ⁠as low.

"Nevertheless, we are not underestimating ‌the threat, which is why all necessary security ​measures have ⁠been activated with minimal ⁠impact on ⁠passengers ⁠and ​airport operations," police said. "After ​landing, ⁠all aircraft will undergo pyrotechnic inspections."
Bulgarian ⁠officials reported three aircraft making emergency landings because of bomb threats.
Airplanes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed in Sofia, the interior ‌minister said, according to broadcaster bTV.
A third aircraft, from London, landed in Plovdiv, local media said.
Polish airlines LOT said on Thursday that a ‌flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely at its ​destination after a ​security warning and no threat was confirmed.

"Following ​receipt of information ⁠regarding a ⁠potential security ‌threat to flight LO235 from Warsaw to Brussels, the flight ⁠crew was notified of the situation and conducted ‌an onboard inspection in accordance with established procedures. No suspicious items ​were found," a LOT ⁠spokesperson said.
Unclear who's responsible for threats
The aircraft landed ⁠at Brussels Airport, ⁠where ⁠security services ​carried out an additional inspection ​of ⁠the plane.
Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome landed safely at Evreux ​airport, 100 km west of Paris, ​after being diverted as a security precaution, the Irish airline said in a statement.
A Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by the Italian air force, a source close to the matter said.
On Tuesday, at least seven flights and a cruise ship received bomb ​threats, causing disruption at airports across Europe, although no devices were discovered.

items: String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe
Another cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps Europe, leaving food spoiled

blocks.text: While ⁠no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at ⁠a time when European officials have been blaming ⁠both Russia ⁠and Iran for what ​they describe as "hybrid attacks" and acts of sabotage. Moscow and Tehran ​both deny any ⁠such campaign.

Drone incursions have periodically forced flight delays and cancellations in Europe and, this week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several countries across the continent. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of low-cost, deniable disruption ⁠efforts.
