articles.title: Will this year’s super El Niño push 2026 to be the warmest year on record?
articles.summary: While the most significant impact on the global temperature typically comes in the months after an El Niño peak — which hasn't happened yet — some climate models are suggesting 2026 could edge out…

image.caption: This map illustrates the temperature anomalies across Earth's oceans. The extreme red in the centre is the current El Niño, with temperatures in some regions reaching as much as 4 C above the average. (Climate Reanalyzer)

blocks.text: Science·New

While the most significant impact on the global temperature typically comes in the months after an El Niño peak — which hasn't happened yet — some climate models are suggesting 2026 could edge out 2024 as the warmest year on record. Could El Niño be influencing this year's global temperature?
Not all climate models suggest 2026 will be the warmest on record
In its monthly temperature update in May, Berkeley Earth, a leading non-profit climate analysis organization, forecast that 2026 had just a 2.5 per cent chance of being the warmest year on record.
Then El Niño started to develop.
The next month it was a 12 per cent chance. By August it had jumped to 69 per cent. Now? Berkeley Earth puts it at a 96 per cent chance.
Is there a link between 2026 potentially being the warmest year on record and this particularly strong El Niño?

This El Niño — a warming in the Pacific Ocean that can contribute to a temporary warming in the global temperature — is already the strongest one since record-keeping began in 1950, beating out the previous record set in 2015-16 by a wide margin.

Scientists consider a strong El Niño to be a warming of 2 C above average. Ocean temperatures in a specific part of the Pacific, near the equator, dubbed “Niño 3.4” reached 3.5 C above average last week.

The ocean temperature in a part of the Pacific Ocean near the equator dubbed Niño 3.4, which is used to measure the strength of an El Niño, is the warmest since records started in 1950. (Climate Central)

Typically, we see the effects of an El Niño on the global temperature about three months after its peak, which is forecast for November or December. However, models show that 2026 will either be the warmest year on record, beating out 2024, or the second-warmest.
“El Niño definitely is leading to the warmth that we're seeing,” said Kent Moore, a professor of atmospheric physics at the University of Toronto.

In its September monthly update, Berkeley Earth reported, "It remains sharply warmer than other months in 2026. September 2026 continued the run of months above the 1.5 C mark that began in July, as the warming influence of El Niño has grown."
But it’s not all El Niño.
Trapped ocean heat

As World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told the Global Heat Forum last month, “El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface.”
And that heat is due to climate change, as we continue to burn fossil fuels, pumping more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

items: 'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
El Niño is here, and it’s already looking like it could be 'mind-blowing'

blocks.text: “The warmth we're seeing in the ocean ... is mostly related to the fact that we've just been warming the ocean up for the last 150 years,” Moore said.
Overall, global ocean temperatures are the warmest they’ve ever been on record, and that’s because the oceans are really good at trapping excess heat.
Ocean temperatures have been the warmest in recorded history. (Climate Central)
And it turns out they’re also really good at trapping CO2. But there are limits.

“As the ocean warms, the amount of carbon dioxide that it can hold is reduced," said Moore. "So, there's a bit of a feedback loop there. As the oceans warm, they become a less efficient sink for carbon dioxide, which means more of the carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere [and it] warms more.”
I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before
So, while El Niño may be playing a small role in 2026's annual global temperature, the main driver is the use of fossil fuels and greenhouse gases released into our atmosphere.

“You got the slow gradual warming of the ocean, and then the El Niño comes along, kicks [around], for six months or so, [and] the temperature goes way up,” Moore said. “And then, of course, El Niño will go away. But of course the warming will still be there.”
Now, not everyone thinks 2026 will beat out 2024 as the hottest year on record.
The U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information gives only a 0.1 per cent chance of it being the warmest and an 86.9 per cent chance of it being the second-warmest.
But 2027's annual global temperature will definitely be more influenced by El Niño.

Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather, writing for Carbon Brief, a climate publication, said, "This year’s record-setting El Niño will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. Carbon Brief projects 2027 at around 1.7 C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96 per cent chance that it will be the warmest year on record."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Habiba Nosheen on her new documentary — and working with Malala
articles.summary: CBC News speaks to documentarian Habiba Nosheen about her new documentary, The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony.

image.caption: A still from Habiba Nosheen's documentary The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony is shown. (Akelo Media)

blocks.text: Entertainment·INTERVIEW
CBC News speaks to documentarian Habiba Nosheen about her new documentary, The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony.
Documentarian speaks about new work, The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony
Habiba Nosheen is no stranger to telling stories through film.

As an investigative reporter (for a time with CBC's the fifth estate) and documentarian, the Emmy- and Peabody-award winning filmmaker has been to war zones, reported on systemic sexual assault and the exploitation of some of the wforld's most vulnerable.

But for her newest work, Nosheen wanted to focus on something different. The result was The Gymnasts of Fisherman Colony, which aired on CBC's The Passionate Eye on Wednesday: a look at three young girls in Pakistan challenging gender norms by training in gymnastics.
While the film also examines systemic issues — the plight of stateless children, denied citizenship or official recognition — it also takes a more personal angle than Nosheen's previous work.
CBC News spoke with Nosheen about crafting the documentary.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Habiba Nosheen on her new doc — and working with Malala
This is a little bit of a different framing than your past work — something more uplifting. Can you talk to me about whether that was intentional or not?
This is the first piece of storytelling that I've ever made that my kids are allowed to watch [laughs]. So it is very much a departure from what I normally do, which is investigative journalism.

I just felt, stepping back and looking at my own body of work, that aspect of joy was lacking. I had not explored spaces and storytelling where you got to see brown women experience joy in a real way. And I wanted to create something that was rooted in that. I mean, I'm not capable of sugarcoating anything. So the film is full of nuance, and there's definitely ups and downs in the lives of these girls that you'll meet in the film. But it's on the lighter side, for sure.

This is such a character-driven piece, particularly these three girls that we follow so closely. Can you speak to me a little bit about going into their world, building that connection? How were you able to get that intimacy, get that connection, get the closeness?

Ten years ago, I adopted my daughter from Pakistan. And the woman who you meet in the documentary, Tahera Hasan — who starts this amazing school that ends up being in this documentary — was my adoption lawyer.

When I found out about this community of stateless children who are struggling to get access to education and sports, I just went to Pakistan, met with them, and I knew I wanted to tell their story. I understand other people, other filmmakers, had approached her over the years who wanted to make this documentary. But I think the fact that Tahera had known me in my other life — as someone who cared about these issues, who cared about girls' rights in Pakistan, independently of my work as a journalist — I think that allowed her to trust me. And that then gave me an in to the community as well.

I did not know about the stateless issues that the Bengali community in Pakistan has been facing. And I live 20 minutes from this community. So I felt like if I don't know, there must be so many others who just don't know anything about this, and this is a story worth telling.

This is such an interesting time for documentary. We're seeing You Can See Everything as one of the biggest movies in the world. Alex Gibney's Musk has generated a huge response, even if it hasn't seen comparable box office success.

As somebody who has made documentaries for years, done journalism for years, what is the experience as a documentarian right now? Is making documentaries, getting them to audiences, more difficult, more easy than it has been in the past?

There are lots of things that technology has made easier when it comes to making the thing that you call a documentary. But in terms of if you want to think about funding and releasing, I absolutely think that there's a huge range. If you want to do documentaries about a celebrity or true crime, there's funding for that. But unfortunately, if you want to make films that are subtitled, that are from a different country, that continues to be a challenge in the arts. I would say across the board, no matter who you are, that's the biggest hurdle we face as documentary filmmakers: telling a story that goes outside the areas that we think the documentary audience is going to want to see.
There are less and less buyers out there for documentaries than there were five, six years ago. So that's made the landscape definitely a lot harder to navigate.

items: Queen of Canada documentary director wants you to know her followers are still out there
Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada

blocks.text: Activist Malala Yousafzai is attached, along with actress Mariska Hargitay. Can you speak to me a little bit about collaboration with some of these names and how that has helped shape the documentary and its journey to audiences?
We're so grateful for the fact that they saw something in this documentary that they would want to lend their names to.

Most of the time, the way it works in documentaries is they came on when the production of it was all wrapped up, and they could see the film. And then when they saw the film before it premiered, they were able to see something that inspired them. And from what I understand, they wanted to lend their name to that. And I find that so touching. Because they're both from very different walks of life. And for them to both want to uplift the stories of these girls in Pakistan has just been such a meaningful journey for us.
I'm curious whether the subjects of this documentary have since seen the documentary, I'm just curious what they think about seeing themselves and their story as it plays out on screen.

Sonia, who's featured in the documentary, was able to come to Tribeca for the world premiere in New York. And right before we were about to go on for the Q&A, she told me that she had never been to a movie theatre before. So the very first film she ever saw was a film about her. I just went 'Good luck trying to follow that!' You know, with Spider-Man or whatever she sees next.

But, you know, it was so beautiful to be able to share that with her and Dara and the space in a theatre. They deserve the visibility and the space that this film gives them because they and their community have been invisible for a really long time. So I just feel privileged that they trusted us to tell their story.

articles.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
articles.summary: Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to…

image.caption: Students work on laptops in the Pedagogical Library at the Free University of Berlin on Sept. 20, 2011. The online resources of academic libraries around the world are increasingly being disrupted by AI bots hunting for content. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.
One school says it was overwhelmed by more than 11,000 searches on Finnish music in just one day

University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents.

"They're just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible," Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News.
The bots are used by both AI and third-party companies to scour websites and retrieve data, often to feed LLMs like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT.
Libraries, museums and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets because they have quality, vetted information that is generally not hidden behind paywalls or logins.

The bots are "causing an incredible amount of work and headache for every institution that does digitization work and every institution that is trying to make information openly available," Strykowski says.
Researchers found such reports started appearing in late 2024 across North America, Europe and Oceania and experts tell CBC News the problem continues to get worse.
LISTEN | Even smarter, with even fewer guardrails:
The Sunday Magazine23:41Inside the global race toward an AI that might kill us all
And new challenges keep arising, says Dean Seeman, director of collections and digital infrastructure at University of Victoria Libraries.
"Sometimes the bot traffic gets so bad that it causes the sites to go down completely for a little while," he said.
Seeman says this creates a "real problem" for public access.

Regular people using library websites are now, effectively, in competition with infinite traffic from bot farms, says Peter Lewis, Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence at Ontario Tech University.

"This is another instance of large, private companies making use of common-good public interest institutions in a way that's very extractive and just assumes that that stuff is available and is free — and then using it to be able to produce highly commercial models that then they can go and sell back to people," he said.

Workers enter data from an old document belonging to the McMillan Memorial Library during a digitization exercise at the Eastland Library in Nairobi on March 24, 2022. Libraries and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets for AI bots. (Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty Images)
Good bots and bad bots

Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed "monstrosities," are "destroying open access" on the internet.
He tells CBC News that "everything's gotten worse" since he wrote that.
Hellman says the problem comes down to good bots and bad bots.

He explains that search engines like Google, and archiving sites like Internet Archive, use bots that follow robots.txt — voluntary sets of instructions on websites that tell them what they can and can't do, so they don't disrupt the site's functioning while gathering information.
AI scraping bots, on the other hand, sometimes ignore these rules and overwhelm websites — in some cases requesting thousands of documents a second and downloading them in every available format.
This is what young people studying artificial intelligence are thinking — as the future of AI grabs headlines

As an example, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported last year that it received more than 11,000 searches for Finnish music from thousands of different internet addresses on the same day. The university said its library catalogue was periodically shutting out students, faculty and staff due to bot traffic.
And because one company or bot farm can work from thousands of IP addresses, Hellman says the old fix of blocking problematic IPs is no longer useful.

Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative effort focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions, is working to protect public access to information. (Submitted by Michael Weinberg)
He says Project Gutenberg is happy for its materials to be used as AI training data and even offers a one-click download of its entire library of books, "but the bots are too stupid to use it."

"Our material is almost all public domain material. It's exactly the sort of material that they should be training on," he said. "We just wish they would do it in a respectful way that doesn't take down websites."
Open access a 'huge benefit'
Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots.

The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions.

Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access to things they believe should be easily accessible.
And as the scraping bots get more advanced, experts say they could also learn to work around these strategies.

The Anthropic logo is displayed at during the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco, on Sept. 17. AI firms have broadly argued that scraping publicly available data is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)
Major AI firms have argued that scraping publicly available data to train their models is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest.

But faced with widespread criticism and copyright lawsuits, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft expressed support last week for honouring a single, standardized opt-out signal in a website's robots.txt file that could block their web crawlers from harvesting data.
Compliance would be voluntary, however, and the agreement leaves out problematic bots from third-party companies and smaller AI startups.

items: Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears
How a small Canadian publisher is resisting the AI book wave
AI is making it harder for voters to get accurate information: Elections Canada chief

blocks.text: Weinberg says the digitization of valuable information has been a "fantastic" development for humanity — giving researchers, teachers and curious citizens easy access to resources that, 20 years ago, "would have required driving for flying or a special permission to get access."
Organizations like GLAM-E are trying to figure out long-term solutions to preserve that access for humans and helpful bots alike.

Right now, the bots create "a disincentive for libraries and other institutions to make parts of their collection available online," Weinberg said. "I think it's been a huge benefit to society that libraries and museums and other cultural institutions have put a huge amount of work into making their collections available."

People look at their laptops and in the main reading room of the New York Public Library on Oct. 5, 2016, in New York City. Increased bot traffic means regular people using library websites are effectively competing with infinite traffic from bot farms, says one expert. (Dominick Reuter/AFP/Getty Images)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Is Grand Theft Auto VI the most anticipated video game of all time? Here are some reasons why
articles.summary: The latest in the long-running series of crime simulators by Rockstar Games is predicted to be the biggest release in video game history.

image.caption: Attendees walk past a Grand Theft Auto VI promotional display at the Sony booth during the Tokyo Game Show 2026 on Sept. 17, 2026 in Chiba, Japan. (Louise Delmotte/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Nick Oulette of Vancouver is one of the millions of video game players around the world anxiously awaiting the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.
"The hype is so real with this one," he told CBC News. "I do think it'll be the game of the decade."

GTAVI, the latest in the long-running series of open-world crime simulators by Rockstar Games, is predicted to be the biggest release in video game history — and not just by hardcore gamers or streamers.

Earlier this month, Steven Adams of the Houston Rockets told media he expects the performance of elite athletes in all major sports leagues to "plummet" as they spend most of their time playing the game instead of training.
Here are some of the reasons why the anticipation for GTAVI has reached a fever pitch.
A mega-popular series
The raw numbers are staggering by any measure.

The series has sold more than 470 million units since 1997, with Grand Theft Auto V alone selling more than 230 million. It remains one of the most-played games on Xbox and PlayStation consoles, thanks to its GTA Online multiplayer mode, according to Circana games industry analyst Mat Piscatella.
According to leaked data released by hackers earlier this year, GTA Online makes Rockstar about $500 billion US every year, or $1.3 million every day.
Lucia and Jason, the main characters of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
Piscatella says 29 per cent of U.S. gamers with a PC or console intend to buy GTAVI at some point, whether at launch or later on down the road.

"If a game gets in the teens-percentage in purchase intent, it's going to be a hit. If it's in the high single digits, it's still really good. But when you're approaching nearly one-in-three, that's kind of off the charts," he told CBC News.
The long wait
GTAVI comes with more than a decade of pent-up anticipation.

Grand Theft Auto V first launched on the PlayStation 3 and Xbox One more than 13 years ago. Development for GTAVI reportedly began around eight years ago. Rockstar only released one major game in the meantime: Red Dead Redemption 2, in 2018.
Rockstar has said very little about the game itself, fuelling a cottage industry of speculation and fake videos purporting to be leaked footage online.
A view of Vice City, one of the playable areas in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

We know the game features two playable characters: Jason and Lucia, a couple juggling their romantic relationship and burgeoning criminal careers in Leonida, the GTA world's satirical version of Florida. But little else about the story, or what players will be able to do, have been teased.
"There is still a lot we don't know about GTAVI, and it's kind of mysterious ... including its budget," said Toronto-based games writer and podcaster Nadia Oxford.
Open-world games with the ambition of GTA are rare, Oxford notes, because they are "horrendously expensive to make" at the production levels expected in today's industry.

Rumours this fall suggested GTAVI's budget surpassed the $1.5 billion US spent to build Dubai's Burj Khalifa skyscraper; Rockstar refuted that claim in interviews with Bloomberg, but did not confirm a price tag.
A gamified life simulator
Oulette estimates he's played GTAV for about 500 hours; much of that time was spent during the COVID-19 pandemic, spending time with his friends online while in lockdown.

"That was a really big contributor to my mental health," he said, "because you could just hop in a car with your buddy and drive down the coast and be like, 'Yeah, how are you doing right now? Are you OK?'"

Oulette says the games' meticulously designed worlds are a cut above others in the same genre, thanks in part to its licensed music, and locations and storylines that satirize real-life pop culture and politics.
"It just kind of makes you feel a little more sane in this insane world when you're playing [this] video game for some reason," he said.
Stephen Totilo, a New Jersey-based games reporter, says that while the GTA games quickly built reputations as a "mayhem simulator," there are plenty of ways to play it without revelling in carnage.
"A lot of people take the GTA games as shock games.... It's the crime, it's the sex, it is the profanity," he said.

"But I think that's only part of what's interesting about what Rockstar is doing, and that what stood out to me ... was this effort to simulate, or even gamify, every aspect that they could think of in the game world."

Early reports have speculated that GTAVI will go even further than past entries, requiring you to fill your car with gas, and eat healthy foods and work out regularly at the gym lest you gain weight that will make you less effective in combat.
Totilo says it will be interesting to see whether keeping up with the "gamified realism simulation" will still be fun for players.
A litany of controversies

The GTA games have a long history of controversies. Oxford points to the moral panic over players' ability to kill civilians, including sex workers, and an infamous sex scene that was cut from 2004's GTA: San Andreas. Players found unfinished files of the interactive sex scene and leaked it online with the nickname "Hot Coffee." The U.S. Federal Trade Commission rebuked Rockstar for not disclosing its existence, even though it wasn't used in the final retail release.
The very first GTA, a top-down game with 2D graphics, got a verbal drubbing in the U.K. House of Lords for its violence, notably the ability to run over pedestrians with a car.

GTAVI has had its own share of controversies even before the release. Hackers have leaked unfinished content from the game, supposedly revealing details like beaches crowded with civilians, Jason cloning a car's FOB to steal it and the ability for players to walk around completely naked.
And some ex-Rockstar workers in the U.K. are taking the company to court because it allegedly fired several employees (including three in Canada) for attempting to unionize.
Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
It's a love story
Beyond the mayhem, carjackings and explosions, Totilo says GTAVI might be the highest-profile love story ever told in a video game.

"There's been plenty of romance in video games before, but nothing of this scale. Nobody has ever put possibly a billion dollars into making a game that appears to be set to be ultimately about a couple," he said, adding that it's also the first time a woman will be a playable main character in a GTA game outside its online modes.
"I think it's a real special moment for the industry and for the culture of games."

articles.title: Alberta's new riding map skews Lethbridge, Banff, Calgary seats toward UCP, voter data suggests
articles.summary: Danielle Smith's MLAs approved a panel's controversial boundary plan over NDP protests.
articles.byline: Jason Markusoff, Joel Dryden, Nael Shiab

image.caption: The UCP-dominated Alberta legislature passed a riding map Wednesday intended to change boundaries for next fall's election. (Juris Graney/CBC)

blocks.text: Alberta’s newly approved political boundary map would tip the Canmore-Banff riding into the United Conservative Party’s win column, pad the governing party’s lead in some Calgary seats and put a UCP-held Lethbridge seat much farther out of contention.

That’s according to a CBC News data analysis that compares how Albertans voted in the 2023 provincial election to the riding layout the UCP-dominated legislature approved Wednesday for the 2027 election.
While the new boundary changes do not put an NDP victory out of reach, it doesn't make it any less of a “gerrymander,” said Feodor Snagovsky, a University of Alberta political scientist.
“The thing about gerrymandering is that it doesn’t have to be this widespread, salamander, American-style thing that totally rigs all election outcomes,” Snagovsky said.
“All it has to be is putting your thumb on the scale and making it more difficult for the other party to succeed.”

The UCP has defended itself against gerrymandering accusations by saying the new map was not drawn by politicians themselves, but rather recommended by an independent advisory panel, composed of a cabinet-appointed former judge, two UCP appointees and two NDP appointees.

But the opposition NDP have argued this was a highly unorthodox process that allowed Premier Danielle Smith’s party to discard the initial commission’s riding plan and replace it with something more favourable to them.
If the last election’s votes were replicated on the advisory panel map that the UCP adopted, 50 ridings would be won by the UCP and 41 by the NDP, based on this analysis.
That’s a narrower gap than the 49-to-38 seat victory achieved by UCP in the last election.
Premier Danielle Smith used this point in question period Wednesday to dispute NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi’s accusations the new map amounts to partisan meddling.
“If his conspiracy theory is that someone gerrymandered the advisory panel's maps to benefit the UCP, then they failed miserably,” she said.

However, the advisory panel's map would produce a bigger victory than would be produced if MLAs accepted the original boundary commission’s map last spring, instead of rejecting it in favour of a second version that aimed to restore two rural ridings proposed for the chopping block and create a 91-riding map.
That discarded map would have produced a five-seat victory for the United Conservatives over the New Democrats, 47 to 42 on an 89-seat map.

In addition to restoring rural seats in central and northern Alberta, the new boundary panel altered the first commission’s Canmore-Banff riding by adding small communities on the Cowboy Trail; fused parts of rural Rocky View County with three west-end Calgary seats; and converted Lethbridge’s two urban seats into one city-only riding and three rural-urban hybrids, with slices of Lethbridge and massive swaths of southern Alberta.

The NDP would have won back that Banff seat by 10.5 percentage points with April’s boundary commission maps, according to CBC News’ transposition of 2023 results by each voting station onto the riding boundaries drawn (then redrawn) this year.
But the newly approved map would flip that seat, giving the UCP a narrow victory margin of 0.7 percentage points.

While the controversial redrawing of Lethbridge wouldn’t lead to any seats switching hands — the NDP currently hold one Lethbridge seat, the UCP the other — it does make it much harder for the NDP to win two seats in the south’s biggest city, and makes the new seat titled “Lethbridge” more competitive between the two parties.
What would have been a 10.8-point NDP victory in Lethbridge-West using the rejected maps becomes a win of half that size in the redrawn Lethbridge seat.

And while the UCP would have held the Lethbridge-East seat with a 1.7-point margin using April’s map, they win each of Lethbridge’s three rural hybrid seats by at least 20.6 percentage points, based on the current seats.

Electoral boundary commissions are tasked with organizing their work around certain factors, including “communities of interest,” referring to groups of people who share certain traits. Snagovsky feels there’s a case to be made that someone living in rural Taber, population 10,000, might disagree that they’re part of a community of interest with someone in Lethbridge, which includes 100,000 people living 50 kilometres away.
“If you're not doing it based around that, then what are you doing?” Snagovsky said.

The majority of the panel argued southern Alberta was united economically around the agricultural and food processing industries, something they said transcended the boundaries of the city of Lethbridge itself.

In Calgary, the effect of adding a few thousand residents of hamlets Springbank and Bearspaw into neighbouring city ridings is comparatively smaller than the changes to Banff and Lethbridge seats. But in every case, it improves UCP fortunes.

A UCP minister was re-elected in Calgary-North West last time by a mere 0.6-point margin, or 143 votes — and the rejected boundary commission kept that map in place. But that UCP margin grows to 1.8 percentage points or 463 votes in the redrawn Calgary-North West-Bearspaw, according to CBC News’ data transposition.
The UCP would have won Calgary-Bow and Calgary-West by larger margins under the old maps, but those leads grow by a few hundred votes in each case.

The majority of the new panel says they chose to remove those hamlet communities from the commission’s proposed Cochrane-Springbank riding and insert them into Calgary because their acreages and rural residences have stronger connections to the 1.5-million person city next door than to the town north of them.
This transposition based on the 2023 election results may or may not be replicated in next October’s provincial elections.

In the Calgary-Shaw byelection in September, the NDP won when votes swung 17 percentage points in their direction (compared to 2023). If the whole next election followed Calgary-Shaw’s trajectory, the NDP could win government on either the rejected commission’s map or the approved panel’s map.
The NDP and UCP were tied for provincial support in the lead-up to the separation referendum, according to a poll conducted in September by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC News.
A tight contest could make some of these tweaks and small partisan advantages in modified ridings even more consequential, according to data scientist and pollster John Santos.

“When you take safe seats for one party, and then you make them marginal or even flip them to the other party, well, that’s exactly why this alternative map has led to accusations of gerrymandering,” said Santos, who works with Brown’s Calgary-based firm.

items: CBC News mapped proposals of Alberta boundary changes to last election results

blocks.text: The initial boundary commission’s chair had recommended striking a new advisory panel if MLAs disapproved of the commission maps and wanted to restore its two eliminated rural districts. However, he recommended against altering any ridings south of Airdrie, which the second panel did with its changes in Banff, Calgary and Lethbridge.
The second panel’s minority members argued that the panel’s map was unfair and unconstitutional.
The majority called such protests “sanctimonious” and incorrect.
The New Democrats have threatened to challenge the ridings in court. No individual or party would be able to file a lawsuit until the new ridings are officially put into force.

articles.title: Pediatrician accused of uploading illicit video of young girl remained licensed for months
articles.summary: Toronto police applications to obtain search warrants obtained by CBC reveal that a tip from Dropbox led to the investigation into 45-year-old Dr. Dilan Dissanayake, who has since been charged with…
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Idil Mussa, Brenda Witmer, Marnie Luke

image.caption: Search warrant applications obtained by CBC News reveal that a Dropbox tip led to the police investigation into Dr. Dilan Dissanayake, a staff rheumatologist at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. Dissanayake, 45, was placed on leave by SickKids in January but did not have his licence suspend

blocks.text: WARNING: This story discusses child sexual abuse material and contains graphic details.
In January, police began investigating a SickKids doctor for allegedly uploading a video depicting child sexual abuse on the Toronto hospital's network.
But it took six months for his medical licence to be suspended, CBC News has learned.

According to Toronto police court filings, officers began investigating Dr. Dilan Dissanayake on Jan. 20, after receiving a tip that suspected child sexual abuse and exploitation material (CSAEM) was uploaded to his personal Dropbox account and logged into with an IP address geolocated to the Hospital for Sick Children.
Police searched his home and office the following week.
In a statement to CBC News, SickKids confirmed that Dissanayake, a staff rheumatologist, was placed on leave on Jan. 28, the day officers searched his office in the SickKids research centre.

"We understand the trust placed in SickKids as a pediatric hospital and the safety of patients, families and staff is paramount. The allegations are deeply disturbing and do not reflect SickKids' values," a spokesperson wrote.
SickKids doctor kept license for 6 months after illicit video probe began, CBC News learns
Dissanayake's medical licence, however, wasn't suspended by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) until July, when he was charged with possessing and accessing CSAEM.
Neither Dissanayake nor CPSO answered CBC's question as to whether he practised medicine in any other context after the investigation began.
This six-month gap troubles Dr. Shannon Ruzycki, a professor at the University of Calgary's medical school.
"If the CPSO hadn't restricted his licence, he could've still been [practising medicine], even if not at the hospital itself," she said.
The allegations against Dissanayake have not been tested in court.
'Pre-teen hardcore' video uploaded: ITOs

The Jan. 20 Dropbox tip was forwarded to Toronto police via the U.S.-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC), a non-profit that receives tens of millions of tips a year from American tech companies, which are mandated to report suspected CSAEM.

CBC News has learned the tip alleged that a file with suspected CSAEM was uploaded to Dissanayake's account in the middle of the afternoon of Jan. 19, according to information to obtain search warrants (ITOs) filed by Toronto police.

According to the unproven affidavits, the file name included the acronym "pthc," which stands for pre-teen hardcore. The detective who reviewed the five-minute video said it shows a female child about 12 to 15 years old, fully nude, being sexually assaulted by an adult man.

In this police application to obtain a search warrant, a Toronto detective describes a 'pre-teen hardcore' video that was allegedly uploaded to Dr. Dilan Dissanayake's personal Dropbox account. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
Police seized seven electronic devices from Dissanayake's home and two computers from his office in the January searches.

In a later ITO to seize a remaining work computer in late February, the detective attested that seven more "thumbcache" images constituting CSAEM were found in an initial examination of the desktop computer seized from his office.
Ruzycki said the alleged behaviour is "repulsive," especially for someone working at a children's hospital.
"That feels worse than if it was just at home," she said. "Not only are you a pediatrician, but you were doing that at work — at work with vulnerable, sick, unwell children."
Doctor questions standard for keeping medical licence
She says that in the interest of protecting vulnerable patients, regulators should err on the side of suspending medical licences when serious allegations arise — even before charges are laid.

"I do think when it comes down to sex- and gender-based violence, crimes that involve children, voyeurism — I think there are certain cases where we have to overreact," said Ruzycki, who led a recent study on physician sexual misconduct.

items: Calgary researchers call for national database tracking physician sexual assault, misconduct

blocks.text: Her research found that the vast majority (85 per cent) of victims of sex- and gender-based violence were women or girls, and nearly six per cent were children.

Asked about Dissanayake's case and when it first learned of the police investigation, the CPSO said it is independently investigating the pediatrician but would not comment further, citing confidentiality provisions.
CSAEM 'depressingly common'

Material like the video described by police depicting sexual activity involving children is "depressingly common," said Monique St. Germain, general counsel for the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, a national organization dedicated to combating child sexual abuse and exploitation.
The incidence of CSAEM access and possession reported to Canadian police has doubled in the past decade, according to StatsCan data.

Canada's share of international online CSAEM tips has likewise spiked. In 2019, approximately 37,000 of the 17 million reports to NCMEC's CyberTipline (0.22 per cent) were geolocated in Canada; by 2025, that number had risen to 129,000 of the 23 million (0.55 per cent) received that year.

"We are at the point now where this needs to be an all-hands-on-deck approach," said St. Germain. "Everybody, including the tech companies, need to be proactively doing things to keep CSAEM off of their platforms."

Monique St. Germain, general counsel for the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, says an 'all-hands-on-deck approach' is needed to combat the spread of child sexual abuse and exploitation material online. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)
SickKids review underway

After a second SickKids employee was arrested in August on child sex crime charges unrelated to those against Dissanyake, SickKids hired KPMG to conduct an external review, and is exploring future "programming" provided by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection.

"We recognize that even the strongest safeguards cannot prevent every instance of alleged criminal conduct. That is why we review our controls and strengthen them whenever possible," the hospital said in a statement.

Toronto police told CBC that "at this time, investigators have found no evidence" that the alleged CSAEM is connected to Dissanayake’s medical practice. It said the investigation is ongoing, however, and anyone with information is urged to contact police.

items: SickKids doctor charged with possessing, accessing child sex abuse material, police say
2nd SickKids staff member charged with possessing, accessing child sex abuse material in less than a month

blocks.text: Ruzycki says even assuming the alleged activity didn't cross into Dissanayake's interactions with his patients, such allegations can hurt families' trust in the medical system.

"I really hope that it never translated to his clinical practice," she said. "But even the perception that it could have, I think really affects how people interact with the medical system, how people trust adults, how people trust their community. I think it really harms us all."
After his arrest, Dissanayake was released on $20,000 bail with restrictions on his internet use and interactions with minors.
His next court appearance is scheduled for Nov. 10.

articles.title: Niagara police investigate 'hate-motivated' vandalism in St. Catharines, Ont.
articles.summary: Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated crime." B'nai Brith Canada says the incident is part of a disturbing trend of…

image.caption: Aleks Goldshtein said his Volkswagen car was badly vandalized after it was towed to a repair shop in St. Catharines, Ont. (Aleks Goldshtein photo)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated crime." B'nai Brith Canada says the incident is part of a disturbing trend of escalating antisemitism in Canada
B'nai Brith Canada says incident reflects growing antisemitism nationally
WARNING: This story includes a picture of a swastika.
Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated" crime.

They say a 2011 grey Volkswagen Passat on Oakdale Avenue was damaged, with its windows broken and hate symbols spray-painted on its side. The car is being examined by the police's forensic unit, they said in a news release.

The release also said that officers are reviewing a social media post relating to this incident and the "Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Unit has been made aware of the incident and will be engaged with the victim."
Aleks Goldshtein said it was his car that was badly vandalized in St. Catharines, though there was no confirmation from police.
Goldshtein, who is Jewish, said he's afraid for his own safety and the safety of his daughter because of the attack.
The human rights organization B'nai Brith Canada said the incident is part of a disturbing trend of escalating antisemitism in Canada.

Goldshtein, who said he is originally from Odesa, Ukraine, and who lived in Israel for five years at one point, sent photos of a grey Passat to CBC that he said is his car, with a swastika spray-painted on the side.

The swastika is widely associated with the Nazi Party of Germany, which among its atrocities during the Second World War committed the systemic murder of six million Jewish people during the Holocaust, along with millions of Roma, 2SLGBTQ+ and other victims.
Car found vandalized at repair shop
Niagara Regional Police said they launched their investigation on Saturday and the car was found vandalized while parked at an automotive repair shop on Oakdale Avenue.
Const. Jessica Martin, a spokesperson, said the police service cannot specify what symbols were spray-painted on the car because it doesn't wish to further spread the use of hate symbols.

On Tuesday, Goldshtein told CBC that his car broke down late at night on Oct. 29 and was towed to a parking lot at a service shop on Oakdale Avenue. He said he left a note in the window about the breakdown, noting he would arrange repairs.
The car had a small Israeli flag attached to the inside of the windshield, he said.

Goldshtein said someone called him the next day to report someone damaging his car. When he went to see it, he saw the extensive damage and the swastika spray-painted on the side. The flag was repositioned into a small hole in the windshield, he said.
Goldshtein said he relied on the car for income, to make deliveries.

Goldshtein says he had this small Israeli flag inside his windshield when it was towed to a repair shop in St. Catharines after a vehicle breakdown. The flag was stuck in a hole in the damaged windshield. (Aleks Goldshtein photo)
He said he's particularly worried because the person or persons who carried out the vandalism may have learned where he lives by ransacking the interior.
"Documents containing my personal information were inside the vehicle, including documents showing my full name, home address and phone number," he said.

"Considering the seriousness of what happened, the exposure of my personal information and the fact that police are now officially investigating the incident as hate-motivated, I believe it is reasonable for me to take my family’s safety very seriously," he said.
"My greatest concern is my daughter. Her safety comes first for me."

items: Reports of hate-motivated crimes are down slightly in Waterloo region, but it's still a pressing problem

blocks.text: Goldshtein said that after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia, his family spent time in Europe, including Germany, before arriving in Canada in 2023 under the Canada–Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel program.
"Canada and the Niagara Region became the place where we tried to rebuild our lives," he said.
Hoping for help to keep safe
Asked by CBC News if he feels less safe in Niagara now, Goldshtein, who didn't want to name the city he lives in, said his sense of safety has been compromised.

"I do not believe that St. Catharines as a community is unsafe, and I have received a great deal of kindness and support from people in Niagara," he said. "[But] what makes me feel unsafe is that I do not know who ultimately committed all of the damage or what information they may now have about me."
He said one of his most urgent needs now is safe and confidential temporary housing, ideally a place where his location would not be publicly known.
"I am willing to relocate to another city or even another province if necessary while the investigation continues."
He hopes victim support programs, Jewish community organizations or other organizations may help him.
Richard Robertson, director of research and advocacy for B'nai Brith Canada, told CBC News on Tuesday that the incident in St. Catharines is not an isolated one.
"It is part of a national crisis of antisemitism. This really is an assault on our nation and its values."
Large rise in antisemitic cases

Robertson said there was a 140 per cent increase in the number of antisemitic incidents between 2022 and 2025, and a 220 per cent increase in the number of violent incidents of antisemitism already in 2026 compared to all of last year

"[It] is not only an affront to the Jewish community; it is contradictory to Canadian values and to the Canada which we all know and love," he said. "That a vehicle could not even be left alone overnight, with an Israeli flag in the vehicle, without the vehicle subsequently being vandalized with hateful antisemitic graffiti, is an appalling testament to the state of hate in this country.

items: London man charged after swastika symbol drawn near homes of Jewish students

blocks.text: "This incident is just yet another disgusting example of how normalized anti-Semitism has become in Canada in 2026."
Niagara police are asking anyone with information about the vandalism to contact them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Some permanent resident applicants left in limbo by changes to Canadian citizenship law
articles.summary: CBC News has learned that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada quietly put permanent resident applications on hold for an unknown number of people who could now qualify for citizenship by…

image.caption: Michel Pottier and his wife Lindsey Jade Higgins are on separate sides of the Canada-U.S. border as a permanent residency application is put on hold due to new citizenship eligibility rules. (Submitted by Michel Pottier)

blocks.text: When Michel Pottier and his wife decided a year ago to move from Maine to his hometown of Halifax, they did their best to plan ahead and play by the rules.
Pottier made arrangements to transfer his job to Canada. His American-born wife, Lindsey Jade Higgins, applied for spousal permanent resident status.
Originally, they expected it would only take a few months. A year later, Pottier has had to begin work in Halifax while his wife is in Portland, Maine, still waiting.

A few days ago, Pottier learned that they could have to wait yet another year to live together in Canada — the result of the way the federal government is implementing changes to citizenship law, Bill C-3, adopted by Parliament late last year.
"We can't be in the same place," said a frustrated Pottier. "That's a difficult pill to swallow — especially since she's so close.… But when it comes to paperwork, you might as well be on the moon."

CBC News has learned that Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada quietly put permanent resident applications on hold for an unknown number of people who could now qualify for citizenship under Bill C-3. The legislation makes those who can prove they have a Canadian ancestor eligible for Canadian citizenship.
That leaves those affected in limbo — without permanent resident status and stuck in a nearly three-year processing backlog of applications for citizenship certificates.

Pottier and his wife applied for her spousal family class sponsorship in September 2025. However, while researching her family tree for that application, they realized that she had a Canadian great-grandmother, which also makes her eligible for Canadian citizenship by descent.
They applied for that as well in October 2025, when there was an interim program that allowed people to apply before the "lost Canadians" legislation formally went into effect.
However, unbeknownst to them, that second application plunged them into the situation they now face.

Initially, IRCC processed her permanent residence application normally, including having her pay for medical tests in January. But a few days ago, Pottier learned through the office of his MP, Justice Minister Sean Fraser, that his wife's permanent resident application was put on hold in September 2026 because she may be eligible for citizenship.

items: Canadians born abroad caught up in yearslong citizenship certificate processing delays

blocks.text: "If we had not applied for the proof of citizenship application, she would have had PR by now," said Pottier. "So, we thought we were doing the right thing, but [we] just destroyed any chance of starting our life in Canada together in any kind of humane timeline."
Pottier said he and his wife are now reconsidering their dream of living in Canada.
Briannah Dale, senior communications adviser for IRCC, said under the department's policies, you can't be both a permanent resident and Canadian citizen at the same time.

"If someone applies for proof of citizenship while also applying for permanent residence, their permanent residence application will be placed on hold while a concurrent citizenship application is assessed," she wrote in an emailed response.

"If citizenship is confirmed, the permanent residence application will be considered withdrawn. If citizenship is not confirmed, the permanent residence application will return to its original place in the processing queue and resume processing."

Dale said an IRCC officer can also put a permanent residence application on hold even if someone hasn't applied for a citizenship certificate if the officer has "compelling reasons to believe an applicant may already be a citizen under Canadian law."
Dale said due to "systems limitations" the department can't say how many permanent residence applications it has put on hold because the applicant may also qualify for citizenship.
However, she said those who already have permanent resident status won't lose their status while they wait for their citizenship certificate.

The wait time for those who apply today for family sponsorship of spouses outside Canada (and outside Quebec) like Pottier's wife is 18 months. But the wait time for citizenship certificate applications is now 34 months, in part because of the surge of applications since the adoption of Bill C-3, particularly from Americans.

Between Dec. 15, 2025, when Bill C-3 went into effect and Aug. 31, IRCC has approved 7,900 applications for Canadian citizenship certificates under the new legislation. Another 22,570 people born abroad to a Canadian parent also received citizenship certificates.
A Canadian citizenship certificate allows the holder to obtain a Canadian passport and live and work in Canada. However, some benefits, like universal health care, have a residency requirement.

items: Demand for Canadian citizenship certificates soaring, fuelled by Americans
Canadian citizenship certificate applications now facing nearly 3-year delays

blocks.text: The demand for Canadian citizenship by descent has been so strong that archives in both Canada and the U.S. have been swamped with requests from applicants for birth certificates and other records to prove Canadian ancestry — some of whom are going back several generations.

In early October, the Association of Canadian Archivists wrote to Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab, calling on the federal government to provide funding and assistance to help archives respond to the increased workload resulting from Bill C-3.
The association has not yet received a response.
Montreal immigration lawyer Lisa Middlemiss says Pottier's family is not the only one trying to navigate IRCC's handling of permanent residence status and Bill C-3.
"The situation comes up more commonly than one might think," she said.

"Frequently we're consulting with individuals who may have a possible claim to Canadian citizenship and recently found out about Bill C-3, however, may also qualify or would normally qualify for permanent residence."
Middlemiss said IRCC hasn't issued any guidance to immigration lawyers on "how to interpret this gray zone."

"The trouble is people are being caught in some sort of processing purgatory, if you will, or limbo, in which they are waiting for a processing of a permanent residence application, which may not happen if they're a Canadian citizen, and they don't also know whether their Canadian citizenship application will be processed urgently."
Citizenship certificate wait times soar to nearly 3 years: IRCC
NDP immigration critic Jenny Kwan said the impact of Bill C-3 on permanent resident status was not something that Parliament contemplated when it debated the legislation.
Kwan said she has been trying unsuccessfully to get answers from Diab's office on behalf of a constituent who is stuck in this limbo.

"I just don't understand why it is so hard for the minister to do her job and to provide that clarity and that confirmation for the general public and to us as members of Parliament representing our constituents," she said.
"The minister, I think, is failing to do her job in implementing Bill C-3."
Diab's office has yet to respond to questions from CBC News.

articles.title: UK can avoid euro but must accept free movement to rejoin EU, says former top Brexit negotiator – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Michel Barnier says Britain could avoid having to join the single currency, but free movement is non-negotiable

Good morning. Andy Burnham is back from the Commonwealth…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham is back from the Commonwealth summit, but the Commons is on mini-recess until Tuesday, and there is not much in the political diary for today. But Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, will be holding a press conference, which means reporters will have the chance to ask him why his eve-of-poll “I don’t go with the consensus that Trump is going to get smashed” prediction turned out to be so wrong.

Another recent claim from Farage has been that, if the UK were to reapply to join the EU, it would have to sign up to the euro. This allegation was never taken particularly seriously by people who actually know how the EU works; while new members are theoretically obliged to sign up to the euro, six of the 27 current members do not use it, one has a formal opt-out (Denmark), and there is plenty of precedent to suggest the EU would easily accept a fudge giving the UK an opt-out.

This morning this has been confirmed by Michel Barnier, who was the lead negotiator for the EU during the Brexit process. In an interview with Cathy Newman for Sky News, he said it would be “perfectly possible to begin such a negotiation [on rejoining the EU] without any kind of obligation to take part in the euro”.
All EU new member states are legally required to join the euro area. However, Barnier said it would be “possible to negotiate a new relationship without this obligation”.

double quotation markBut what is, and what remains unnegotiable, is the condition to join the single market. There is no negotiation possible. No possible negotiation on any kind of cherry-picking or the single market ‘a la carte’. The UK knows quite perfectly the condition to be part of and to rejoin the single market and the customs union.
But the EU would not compromise on free movement, Barnier said:
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, and Sir Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, are questioned by the London assembly.
Noon: The Bank of England announces its decision on interest rates. They are expected to go up.
2pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, holds a press conference with Danny Kruger, how is in charge of the party’s preparations for government.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Who is Rodil Zalameda, the 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court
articles.summary: Rodil Zalameda is the country's 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court, replacing Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 4:46pm
Rodil Zalameda is the country's 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court, replacing Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6.

Before President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. picked him to lead the country's highest tribunal, Zalameda served as an SC associate justice appointed by then-President Rodrigo Duterte on August 6, 2019.
He penned the SC First Division decision, made public on September 9, 2026, overturning the graft conviction of former First Lady Imelda Marcos.
He also penned the SC En Banc decision in 2023 granting a writ of amparo in favor of former Bayan Muna lawmaker Siegfred Deduro.
Zalameda also served as an associate justice of the Court of Appeals from 2008 to 2019 and chairperson of its 17th Division.
He also worked as a city prosecutor and public prosecutor in Mandaluyong City and a branch clerk at the Makati City Regional Trial Court.

The new SC chief justice obtained his Bachelor of Laws degree at Ateneo de Manila University in 1987 under an academic scholarship grant. According to Zalameda's profile posted on the SC website, he was an associate editor of the Ateneo Law Journal, a senior staff member of the Ateneo Law Bulletin, and a member of the Fraternal Order of Utopia.
He passed the Bar examinations in 1988.

He earned his secondary education from the University of the East Caloocan in 1979 and his Bachelor of Arts major in Political Science degree from UE Manila in 1983. UE recently conferred Zalameda the honorary Doctor of Laws degree.
Zalameda was also recognized as one of UE's Outstanding Alumni twice.
In 2006, Zalameda was among the 10 Outstanding Pillars of Justice of the Rotary Club of Diliman.
He also received the Ulirang Mandaleño Award of the Mandaluyong government under the Government Category in 2010.
The Ateneo Law Alumni Association Inc. also bestowed Zalameda the Distinguished Alumni Award under the Judiciary Category in 2022.
Zalameda is born in Caloocan City. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: DA to sustain subsidies, lower tariffs to reduce food supply chain costs
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Thursday it will pursue interventions to slash food supply chain costs as inflation rose to 7.8% in October.

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 4:33pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Thursday it will pursue interventions to slash food supply chain costs as inflation rose to 7.8% in October.
The department said it will continue providing fuel and toll subsidies, financial aid, farm inputs, crop insurance, and reduced tariffs on essential animal feed components like corn.
Among the initiatives by the DA is the expansion of the government’s P20 per kilo rice program for the vulnerable sector.

“We are also expanding the coverage of Benteng Bigas, Meron Na!, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s affordable rice program, to help shield vulnerable households, including those with senior citizens, solo parents, and persons with disabilities, from price pressures arising from external shocks beyond the government’s control,” said DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. in a statement.

Food inflation —which tracks the price movements of food items in a “basket” commonly purchased by households— saw a slight decrease of 6.4% from 6.8%, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
The PSA said the downtrend in food inflation in October was mainly driven by the slower annual increases in the indices of Fish at 5% from 7.4%, and in Vegetables at 5.7% from 10.5%.
Rice remained the largest contributor to overall inflation, while transport and energy costs recorded some of the sharpest increases amid rising fuel prices.
Moreover, Tiu Laurel noted that affordable food depends on a steady supply, warning that climate impacts and geopolitical conflicts continue to jeopardize global and local agricultural production.
“Keeping food prices manageable requires not only bringing down costs but also ensuring that farmers can continue producing enough to meet domestic demand,” the DA said in a statement.

To address price pressures, the Department of Economy, Planning and Development said the government is strengthening agricultural production and logistics while providing targeted assistance to sectors affected by higher energy costs. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: The new chief justice: Who is Rodil Zalameda?
articles.summary: This marks the second appointment of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to the Supreme Court and the first to the position of chief justice.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 4:29pm
Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda on the sidelines of an Integrated Bar of the Philippines in Roxas City in August 2023.
SC PIO
MANILA, Philippines — A new chief justice has been appointed, filling the highest post in the judiciary as Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo reaches compulsory retirement on November 6.
This marks the second appointment of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to the Supreme Court and the first to the position of chief justice.
On November 5, Presidential Communications Office chief Lino Cayetano announced that Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda had been appointed to the highest post in the judiciary.
He was chosen over two other senior justices appointed by the late President Benigno Aquino III, namely Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.
Other shortlisted candidates included former President Rodrigo Duterte's detained associates, Associate Justices Japar Dimaampao and Jose Midas Marquez.
What will be Zalameda’s role?

The 1987 Constitution does not mandate any formal role for the chief justice other than serving as an ex-officio chairman of the Judicial and Bar Council and presiding over any impeachment trial of the president.

Despite holding the highest position in the judiciary, his vote carries the same weight as those of the other justices, with only 1 vote out of 15, as he is considered “first among equals” and not superior to the other justices.
He is also required to personally certify every decision rendered by the court.
Who is Zalameda?
Zalameda graduated from Ateneo de Manila University School of Law in 1987. He passed the Bar Examinations in 1988.
According to reports, after passing the bar, Zalameda worked as a clerk at the Makati Regional Trial Court for two years.
He then entered private practice before returning to government service in 1995 as a prosecutor in Mandaluyong. He became assistant city prosecutor in 1997 and city prosecutor in 2002.
RELATED: NCR chief prosecutors endorse Zalameda for chief justice
He served in the position until his appointment to the Court of Appeals on Sept. 5, 2008.
In 2019, Duterte appointed Zalameda as an associate justice of the Supreme Court, replacing Associate Justice Mariano del Castillo, who retired on July 29, 2019.
He was the first Supreme Court appointee to take a decision-writing exam in addition to an interview conducted by the Judicial and Bar Council.
Notable decisions penned by Zalameda
During his stint as an associate justice, Zalameda penned several notable decisions.

Zalameda was the ponente in the Deduro vs. Vinoya decision in 2023, which declared that red-tagging is a threat to life, liberty and security and that individuals being red-tagged can avail themselves of the writ of amparo.

He also penned the June 2026 decision acquitting former First Lady Imelda Marcos. Zalameda acquitted the former first lady of seven counts of graft involving Swiss foundations, reversing a 2018 Sandiganbayan decision.
RELATED: What Supreme Court's Imelda Marcos acquittal means, and what it doesn't

Zalameda also wrote a 2023 ruling stating that a minor above 15 but below 18 may still be criminally liable if the prosecution proves that the child acted with discernment. In this case, Zalameda upheld a homicide conviction.

articles.title: LIST: VP Sara’s witnesses for Nov. 9–13 hearings
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers have submitted a witness lineup for the Senate impeachment proceedings.

blocks.text: Headlines
November 5, 2026 | 3:58pm
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte shows a document after posting bail at a court building in Quezon City suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers have submitted a witness lineup for the Senate impeachment proceedings, in which they plan to call bank officials and city assessors to address the remaining charge against her of alleged unexplained wealth.

In a statement on Thursday, November 5, impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said the defense filed two manifestations on November 4 asking the court to subpoena 25 individuals for hearings from November 9 to 13.
Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero will act on the requests based on the court’s rules and its standards on relevance and admissibility, Tongol said.
The court also said the trial would go ahead despite a pending Supreme Court challenge to the voter threshold issue.

Through the Office of the Solicitor General, the Senate has asked the High Court to throw out a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go — both allies of Duterte — and to deny their plea for a restraining order.
First witness declines to appear
The defense’s planned first witness however — Ralph Sarmiento, a former law dean at the University of St. La Salle in Bacolod City — has asked to not be called to the stand.
Sarmiento, who was scheduled to testify Monday on constitutional principles relevant to Article II, said that he was declining “to preserve the independence of my constitutional law scholarship.”
Defense spokesperson Michael Poa said the team respected the decision.

The remaining charge, Article II, accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth, failing to fully declare her and her husband’s assets in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN), and retaining business interests barred by the Constitution.
House prosecutors dropped the three other articles — on confidential funds, bribery and grave threats — when they rested their case on October 13.
Here is the defense’s list of intended witnesses for November 9 to 13, according to the impeachment court:

articles.title: Who is Dean Ralph Sarmiento, tapped by Sara Duterte's camp as witness
articles.summary: Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento was listed as Vice President Sara Duterte"s first witness at her impeachment trial. He, however, decided to decline to participate as a witness a day after the…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 3:44pm

Law professor Dean Ralph Sarmiento was listed as Vice President Sara Duterte’s first witness at her impeachment trial. He, however, decided to decline to participate as a witness a day after the announcement was made.
So who is Sarmiento, and why was he called to become a witness for the Vice President?

On his Facebook profile, Sarmiento listed several educational institutions he attended. In 1992, he received his Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science at University of Negros Occidental – Recoletos.

He earned his Juris Doctor degree at the University of St. La Salle (USLS), where he would spend most of his professional career. Sarmiento graduated Magna Cum Laude from USLS and placed 10th in the 1997 Bar Exams, according to publisher Centralbooks, where the law professor has two books.

In 2002, Sarmiento also studied Classical Works and Scholarly Approaches to the U.S. Constitution as a Fulbright Institute fellow at Temple University in the United States, according to his Facebook profile.
Sarmiento would also go on to study Constitutional and Territorial Reforms in Federal Switzerland as a Swiss Institute of Federalism scholar at the University of Fribourg in 2008.
According to Sarmiento’s LinkedIn page, he has over 28 years of experience working as a law professor at the USLS, where he held various positions.

From June 1998 to May 2010, he was the executive director of the school’s Law Center. From 2010 to 2016, he was the university’s College of Law Dean. He took the position once more from August 2023 to January 2026.

By October 2025, he became the USLS’s Vice Chancellor for Administration. While both his LinkedIn and Facebook profiles still list him as presently working as a vice chancellor, Duterte’s defense team labeled him a “former Vice Chancellor for Administration.”
Sarmiento has over 318,000 followers on Facebook.
During Duterte’s trial, Sarmiento has offered his legal opinions on the matter to several news outlets. Many of his views, however, could also be found online.

“We should hold VP Sara Duterte accountable for every peso of public money and every act properly charged against her. But accountability loses its moral force when fairness is sacrificed. Due process is not a favor to the accused. It is what makes accountability credible,” Sarmiento said in a Facebook post on October 14.

“The Constitution does not ask us to choose between accountability and due process. It demands both, and I support both. I support accountability. I also support due process. We should not have to choose between the two. The stronger the accusation, the greater the need for a complete and tested record,” he added.
The post came a day after the House prosecution dropped three out of the four articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Duterte’s defense team decried the dropping of the cases, as it did not give them a chance to defend the Vice President. —AOL, GMA News
