articles.title: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.summary: Authorities in British Columbia say evidence suggests an animal may have been involved in the women's deaths.

blocks.text: A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.

The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.

He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC, external.
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.summary: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.byline: Joel Guinto, Kurumi Mori, Darren Bett

blocks.text: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
Image source, Getty Images
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin
ByJoel GuintoBBC NewsReporting fromSingaporeKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Darren BettLead weather presenter
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
Typhoon Champi hit Taiwan and Japan
Source: NASA
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra

blocks.text: Image source, VCG via Getty Images
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.

blocks.caption: Graphic showing the track of Typhoon Dolphin towards eastern China in August 2026.

blocks.text: 'Burning with fever'

The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.

blocks.caption: Graphic showing the track of Typhoon Champi towards Taiwan and Japan in October 2026.

blocks.text: The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.

Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies
'Very, very scary' simulations

In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.

To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.

They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.

In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains
Preparing for the onslaught

Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.

"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

articles.title: Democrats take House and Senate from Republicans in US midterm rout
articles.summary: Democrats will control both chambers of Congress after flipping seats in Republican strongholds across the US in an election seen as a repudiation of President Donald Trump.

image.caption: Texas is sending a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since 1988Image: Mike Segar/REUTERS

blocks.text: By late Tuesday night, it was clear that Democrats had succeeded in turning the 2026 US midterm elections into the so-called "blue wave" that had been predicted by pollsters.
But by Wednesday morning, the scale of the victory had turned into a "blue tsunami," surprising even the most optimistic political pundits.
In January, Democrats are set to have a commanding majority of at least 237 to 139 in the House and a 54 to 44 advantage in the Senate.
Democratic candidates flipped seven highly competitive Senate seats, including in what have for decades been reliably Republican districts in "red" states.
Texas voted in James Talarico as its first Democratic Senator since 1988, while electing a Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, for the first time in over 30 years.
The heartland state of Kansas, where farmers have been hit by high diesel prices and tariffs, will send a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in over 90 years.
Other surprise wins in Republican strongholds included Iowa, South Carolina, and Ohio.
Big Democrat victory in US midterm elections

According to data analyzed by the New York Times, the 2026 Democrats came in at a 13 point margin of victory over the Republicans for the popular vote in the House, the largest such margin since 1976 seen in the wake of the Watergate scandal that shattered the presidency of Republican Richard Nixon two years prior.

Democrats also saw large gains in almost every voter group compared with the 2024 presidential election that put Trump in the White House, indicating the breadth of the political swing away from Republicans.
The full scale of the Democrat majority in both chambers may not be known until later Wednesday or Thursday as some races are still too close to call, or take longer to count ballots.
Democrats promise change, buoyed by Trump's unpopularity
The midterms were seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump, who had historically low approval ratings of around 38% ahead of election day.
Trump had campaigned relentlessly in the weeks leading up to the election, in what often turned into meandering speeches to dwindling crowds.

Democrats were able to capitalize on Trump's unpopular policies like the war in Iran and ensuing record-high fuel costs, which compounded a growing affordability crisis while the president was seen as enriching himself.
On Wednesday, Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party was focusing "relentlessly on affordability and on accountability."

"The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over," said Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker of the House in January.
Democrats say they are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower costs for fuel, groceries and healthcare, while conducting vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration.
When asked about the option of impeaching Trump or cabinet members for breaking laws while in office, Jeffries said Democrats were not focusing on that for now.
The margin of victory in the Senate is still not a two-thirds supermajority, with which Democrats alone could vote to convict in cases of impeachment, or override presidential vetoes.
Even as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term, Trump still has the power of the executive at his disposal, which comes with broad sway, especially in foreign policy.
Midterms put US political divide on display
GOP blame game begins

Despite for months claiming that Democrats would cheat to win the election, Trump did not dispute the Republican blowout. Instead, he claimed that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot.
Nevertheless, Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats, while at the same time promised to use veto power to block legislation.
In remarks on Wednesday outside of his ballroom construction site at the White House, Trump appeared to admit that the economic impacts of the Iran war had cost the Republican Party.

blocks.caption: Trump preferred to speak more about ballroom project than the midterms on WednesdayImage: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump said.
Earlier Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance was more direct, saying the Iran war was the "reason we lost."
However, Trump spent the majority of the time in front of reporters on Wednesday talking about his ballroom project.
"It's going to be not only one of the biggest, but it'll be the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world," he said.
Republican supporters react: People are voting out of 'anger'

articles.summary: Aiwanger was Bavaria's economic minister and the chairman of the Free Voters Party. The circumstances surrounding his death are still unclear.

image.caption: Aiwanger often espoused populist rhetoric [FILE: Sept 3, 2023]Image: Uwe Lein/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, according to German media reports. He was 55 years old.
Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party.
What do we know about Hubert Aiwanger's death?
The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear.
Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.

articles.title: Winners, losers, the EU: Five takeaways from the US midterms
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, with the Democrats wresting control of Congress. What does this mean for US politics and the world?

image.caption: Donald Trump's power has been diminished now that the Democrats control CongressImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: The Democrats not only made significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections but also took control of both chambers of Congress. Here are five insights that can be drawn from this moment.
1. US democracy is alive and well

The storming of the Capitol, attempts to change the rules of the electoral process, a spate of presidential executive orders to bypass Congress and many more examples sparked concerns that the US' vaunted democracy was being transformed into an authoritarian system under Donald Trump. But the country's democratic institutions have proven more resilient than many had feared.
Many voters were driven by their opposition to Trump's desire to rule with unfettered power. Instead they want to see country's institutional safeguards strengthened.

A post-election survey by news agency Associated Press found that about 30% of voters thought the state of democracy was the country's biggest problem. About 70% felt that Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the president.

This midterm result sends a clear signal that voters want stronger parliamentary oversight. President Trump could of course continue trying to govern through executive orders, bypassing Congress. But Congress sets the budget.

This means the Democrats, who now control Congress, can deny the president the funds he needs for his political initiatives. They can also set up investigative committees, which puts the Trump government under considerable pressure to justify its actions.
2. The Democrats can still win elections

For a long time, the Democratic Party lacked compelling leadership, a unified approach and a clear answer as to how it intends to win votes. Tuesday's election proves the party is still a political force to be reckoned with.

Its gains in many Republican strongholds are nothing short of sensational. The party was even able to score victories in Texas and South Carolina. In Kansas, the Democrats won a Senate seat for the first time since 1932.
The midterms have also put the spotlight on a new generation of Democrats: Younger politicians, some of them noticeably more progressive, who could chart a fresh course for the party.

Take, for instance, the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, an organization which is considerably more left-wing than the Democratic Party itself. At least five candidates endorsed by the DSA have been elected to the House of Representatives.

blocks.caption: James Talarico becames the first Democrat to win a Senate seat for Texas Senate in over 30 yearsImage: Eric Gay/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The DSA advocate for strong welfare policies that focus on affordable housing, health care and workers' rights. They also want to see greater checks on the power of large corporations.

"The argument was always that these folks can't win on a national stage," Brandon Bohrn, an expert on trans-Atlantic relations at the Bertelsmann Foundation, told DW. Now some of them have defied the odds and actually won, potentially sparking an internal debate about what the Democrats stand for and how they plan to win voters in the 2028 presidential election, Bohrn said.
3. The Republicans face a fierce internal battle over the party's future
Donald Trump has already made it clear that he does not hold himself responsible for this midterms defeat, taking to Truth Social to deflect any blame.

Yet not everyone in the Republican party is likely to agree. Critics of Trump who had been sidelined may feel emboldened to speak up again. The question as to whether the Republicans should abandon Trumpism will be almost impossible to ignore.

By law, Donald Trump cannot run for a third term in the 2028 presidential race so Republicans will have to think about who can. But who will take the lead? And more importantly: On what policy platform?
Tuesday's election defeat will likely accelerate this debate, making a power struggle over the Republicans' political future inevitable.
4. For Iran's leadership, Trump's defeat is good news
The war against Iran and resulting economic hardships have cost the Republicans many votes. The cost of living, in particular, was a key issue for many American voters.
The consequences of the Iran war have primarily driven up energy prices. This is likely to significantly increase domestic pressure on Trump to reach a lasting agreement with Iran.

Trump does seem keen to cut foreign policy costs, especially in areas where it has been politically controversial for his party. Shortly before the midterms, he announced that he no longer intends to provide billions in military aid to Israel. This was in relation to a deal that was meant to expire in two years anyway.
5. What the election outcome could mean for Europe

Ian Lesser, an expert on US foreign and security policy at the German Marshall Fund, believes that the midterm elections could also impact trans-Atlantic relations. "This actually makes a big difference for Europe in a number of different important ways," Lesser told DW.

blocks.caption: Trump has not shown great enthusiasm for NATOImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Democrats could try to reinvigorate dialogue between Europe and the US, Lesser suggests. After all, with control of Congress, the Democrats have more say on Trump's NATO policy, can influence budget decisions and military funding, and can complicate planned cuts to US support. Europe and the US may even cooperate on climate and environmental issues.
"Simply restoring a degree of trust and predictability, however we get to that, makes a big difference," Lesser said.
Not all differences will be resolved overnight though.

"Tariffs are a little tricky because there are clearly vested interests in the US in keeping some of this in place," Lesser concluded. "But in terms of new and very aggressive tariff measures, I think Congress would absolutely push back against that, on both sides of the aisle, actually."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Mother and daughter both killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm
articles.summary:
Conservation officers say the women reported missing over the weekend, were found near a trail near their home

Search teams in Canada…

blocks.text: Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.

“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service is probing the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.

Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.

A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.

“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.

Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.

Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.

Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

articles.title: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files
articles.summary: Decades after the end of Soviet rule, Hungary is releasing all its secret service files. The disclosure is sparking fresh debate about informants, guilt and responsibility.

image.caption: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar made releasing the documents a campaign pledgeImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.

blocks.caption: In 1956, Hungarians tried to stop Soviet tanks with cobble stone barricades Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.
Release opposed for years

Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.

Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.

A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.

The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.

Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.

blocks.caption: Viktor Orban's Fidesz party never supported making the 'agent files' publicImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Political fallout expected
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.

Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.

The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.

Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.

Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."

blocks.caption: Defendants are questioned by a judge in Budapest on March 9, 1957, during the first show trial held after the 1956 Hungarian uprisingImage: MTI/picture alliance

blocks.text: Political reckoning
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.

When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.

Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship
articles.summary:
Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his…

blocks.text: On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship has become a political liability.

Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.

Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinian, been widely been described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.

Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.

Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.

“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.

The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.

“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”

Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipa pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.

The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.

“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

In Michigan, El Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.

For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said . “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”

Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.

“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: Will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

articles.title: Canada-U.S. trade minister says Democrats' midterm landslide doesn't change Ottawa's strategy

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump are seen together in June. Both leaders have said in recent days that trade talks are ramping up again. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's point man on the Canada-U.S. trade file says the federal government's strategy isn't changing in the short term despite American voters handing a seismic win to Democrats in Tuesday night's midterm elections.
LeBlanc says Canada still must work with president and his cabinet

While the results are widely seen as a strong repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump and his economic policies, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc wouldn't weigh in ahead of a caucus meeting on Wednesday morning in Ottawa.

"It's not particularly constructive for Canadians to interpret results in a foreign country's election," he said. "Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that's to work with the people that Americans have elected."
LeBlanc noted the trade talks are conducted with Trump and his cabinet.

items: Trump says it's 'largely true' Iran war led to Republican midterm losses

blocks.text: "They remain in office today. And those are the people with whom we'll be having those conversations," he said.
Canada has been seeking a trade deal with the U.S. in hopes of lowering steep tariffs on Canadian goods, including targeted sectors like autos, steel, aluminum and softwood.
'Our focus hasn't changed,' LeBlanc says as Democrats take U.S. Congress

One of the big questions for the Canadian side is how the infamously volatile U.S. president reacts to the midterm shellacking, one that delivered control of both the House and Senate to Democrats, and whether it gives Prime Minister Mark Carney's government more leverage.
Trump was already signalling some movement on the file, telling Fox News on Tuesday morning he was close to a deal.

Carney didn't go quite as far but told reporters that afternoon that the White House has shifted its stance on some of what he called Canada's "red lines," including language requirements and Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
'We've made progress' with U.S. on trade talks, Carney says
"They're asking less and they're offering more," the prime minister said, adding the two leaders will meet in China later this month.
He said there is still work to be done before a deal is inked. Autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.
Trump still has his veto powers
A blue Congress doesn't necessarily mean it's clear sailing for Canada.
The new crop of representatives and senators won't be sworn in until January, and even after that Trump will still be able to lean on his executive authority.
After the results came Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-style hat with the word "VETO," although he also told Politico "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything."

LeBlanc said "what the new Congress might decide to do when they're seated two months from now is an interesting discussion," but that's "not going to change the work that we have to do in the next two weeks."
"The American Congress will act in the interests of the American Congress. Our work will be focused on what we can do here at home," he said.

items: What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada
Carney says U.S. 'asking less and offering more' with 'more intense' trade talks underway

blocks.text: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it's on Carney and his government to leverage the results to land a tariff-free trade deal with the U.S. administration.

"Americans hate these tariffs," he said. "Let's leverage that goodwill to pressure the administration and Congress to remove all the tariffs, lower the cost of living for Americans but also boost jobs and business for long-struggling Canadians."
Ford 'doing cartwheels'
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most colourful critics of Trump's tariffs at the premiers' table, said he "was doing cartwheels down the street" as the votes were being tallied.
"You ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels? I was jumping up and down when the results were coming in. But it's very simple, the American people spoke," he said.
Doug Ford 'doing cartwheels' over U.S. midterm results
Ford said he'll be reaching out to governors and is instructing his cabinet to reach out to U.S. Congress members and senators.
"The war is not over. We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board," he said.
Former ambo urging caution
Canada's former ambassador to the U.S., Kirsten Hillman, cautioned the federal government against making any sudden changes.

"If they're having constructive conversations that are heading towards some kind of arrangement that would work for Canada, we wouldn't want them to stop that," Hillman said during election night coverage on CBC News.
Former Conservative cabinet minister James Moore suggested Carney shouldn't accept a deal with tariffs now.

"Americans don't want tariffs. The polls and voters are clear. Do not make a deal with a repudiated and departing president that normalizes tariffs that Americans and Canadians don't want," he posted on X.
"Do not put Canada at an economic disadvantage with a tariff-accepting deal."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca
With files from Mike Crawley

articles.title: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
articles.summary: Democrats can vote legislation through. But Trump still has veto power.

blocks.text: Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.
They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.
"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.

After months of promises on the campaign trail — to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war — they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.

A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.
The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".
"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."
Congressman Robert Garcia of California will soon lead a powerful oversight committee in the House, with the power to make Trump's last two years in office quite difficult.
"Lawyer up," the Democrat said in a statement as victorious results poured in on election night.

Committees in both the US Senate and House have investigative powers, which they could use to delve into alleged conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him. On Tuesday, Garcia rattled off a list of possible targets: Trump's family, "corporate corruption", alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the government's handling of the Epstein files.
The Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations.

Should a US Supreme Court vacancy, for example, arise during Trump's term, Senate Democrats could use their new power to block a nomination - or force Trump to choose a more moderate candidate who garners bipartisan support.
The House also has the power to impeach a president - the first step of Congress' process to remove an official from office.

Democrats twice impeached Trump during his first term, though the US Senate eventually voted to acquit him in both cases. But because it takes a two-thirds majority in the US Senate — or 67 votes — convicting a president in an impeachment case likely will remain out of reach for Democrats.

There's an active debate among Democrats about whether impeachment is a good idea. The first impeachment, in 2019, unleashed partisan rancor and allowed Trump to cast himself later as a victim of political persecution, which later helped build support for his second White House run.
Jeffries, who would almost certainly have to greenlight any Democratic impeachment effort, has kept his plans vague.
"Well, we've made clear: We haven't ruled anything in," he told CNN in August. "And we haven't ruled anything out".
Americans' frustration with Congress' productivity was palpable before the election. Only 14% of US registered voters approved of lawmakers' performance, an October Gallup poll suggested.
But with a Republican in the White House and Democrats running Congress, Americans may face even more deadlock.

"If you thought legislating was hard in the last Congress with unified Republican control, that will get much more complicated," said Casey Burgat, professor of legislative affairs at George Washington University.
Because they will control both chambers with a comfortable majority, Democrats will be able to pass legislation through Congress with relative ease.
Getting it enacted into law will be harder.

A president must sign most legislation in order for it to become law. Trump has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress that he does not support, and Congress can only override him with a supermajority from both chambers - margins Democrats alone will not have despite their success on Tuesday.
As his party lost Senate race after Senate race Tuesday night, Trump struck a conciliatory tone with the New York Times.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," he said.

But a few minutes later, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of his red campaign hat with the word "VETO" emblazoned across the front. That Jekyll-and-Hyde approach to a Democratic Congress could become a theme.
While opposition to Trump led to Democrats' success, lawmakers acknowledged Tuesday night, it might not be enough.
"It is overwhelmingly a rejection of Donald Trump, and his agenda and policies," Coons told the BBC.
"But if we overreach, or if we fight too much internally, we could miss this moment."

Despite the veto threat, Jeffries has said that his party wants to restore significant cuts Republicans made to healthcare programmes like Medicaid, which is used by low-income groups, and the Obamacare marketplace.
"We're committed as a top priority as House democrats to reversing these Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a September event for healthcare workers.

On typically bipartisan issues – such as policies affecting affordability, regulating the AI industry, re-evaluating military funding for Israel and reining in the Iran War – talks could break down as lawmakers try to compromise. As they become the opposition heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, Republicans might not be in the mood to help Democrats achieve too many wins.

Fissures also could erupt even among Democrats themselves, particularly on matters involving Israel, that may make party consensus difficult. A schism emerged in the Democratic Party during the midterms over continued US military funds for Israel.

Incoming senators like Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and some incoming members of the US House, said during the campaign they would vote for legislation to curtail aid to Israel. These Democrats could face a road block from their own leadership.
Then there's the matter of reining in Trump's foreign policy, which could be difficult, despite Democrats' majority.

Even before the midterms, Congress saw bipartisan efforts to limit Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran. Though some of these measures passed one or both chambers, Congress has not been able to enforce them. Notably, both the House and the Senate passed a resolution in June to halt hostilities with Iran, which Trump could not veto but has essentially ignored.

The White House has argued Trump has broad powers to continue the war. But Congress' authority to force Trump's hand is an "open legal question," said Scott Anderson, senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution.
"Congress can try to litigate this out, and force the courts to tell us."

articles.title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
articles.summary: At least 40 people were killed and another 30 may still be under the rubble after Monday's attack on a Ukrainian village, Kyiv says.

blocks.text: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.
It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.
Severely damaged buildings are also seen.
A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha.
"Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.
Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops.
Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.
BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.
In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians.
"First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."

The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.
Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify

articles.title: The 2011 discovery of neo-Nazi killers aired biases in German policing
articles.summary: Many questions still surround the National Socialist Underground whose existence was revealed by neo-Nazi terrorist Beate Zschäpe on November 4, 2011. How has German society reacted to NSU crimes?…

image.caption: The memorial plaque for 10 NSU murder victims in KasselImage: Uwe Zucchi/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Halit Yozgat was killed at point-blank range on April 6, 2006, in Kassel, in the German state of Hesse. Before him, eight other men with immigrant backgrounds had also been shot point-blank since September 2000. The 10th and final person killed by the group Germany would come to know as the National Socialist Underground did not fit this pattern: She was a woman. Police officer Michèle Kiesewetter was killed by the NSU on April 25, 2007, in Heilbronn, in the German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Four and a half years after Kiesewetter's death, the identities of the people behind the murders came to light. On November 4, 2011, Beate Zschäpe, who is now imprisoned with little likelihood of release before 2035, revealed the existence of the NSU. The group also included Uwe Böhnhardt and Uwe Mundlos, who were found dead in a burned-out RV on the same day.

The two men are believed to have died in a murder-suicided following a failed bank robbery in the eastern German city of Eisenach, under circumstances that have never been fully clarified. In a macabre confession video that Zschäpe sent to the media, they boasted that they had shot and killed nine men on racist grounds.
Second NSU trial ends with suspended sentence

One of the many unanswered questions is why Kiesewetter was also killed. No definitive answers were provided either in the first NSU trial before a Munich court, which lasted from 2013 to 2018, or in numerous parliamentary investigative committees.

blocks.caption: A woman who helped Beate Tschäpe received a suspended sentence Image: Sebastian Kahnert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fifteen years after the neo-Nazi terrorist group was exposed, the families of the murder victims are increasingly losing hope that any new information will come to light. One such opportunity was the trial of Susann Eminger — who was sentenced in July by a court in Dresden, in the state of Saxony, to two years of probation for supporting the terrorist group.

Eminger helped Zschäpe assume a different identity during doctor's visits and when dealing with the police by letting Zschäpe use her health insurance card and ID card. However, the court was unable to prove that she was aware of the series of murders committed by the NSU.

Relatives of the murder victims and the survivors of a nail-bombing carried out by the NSU in the western city of Cologne say the verdict beggars belief. "Ten people were executed in cold blood, and countless others were injured in bombings," said Michalina Boulgarides, whose father, Theodoros, was shot dead in Munich on June 15, 2005.

blocks.caption: The NSU murdered 9 men of immigrant background and one womanImage: Norbert Försterling/Polizei-Handout/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "When will the victims get justice?" Boulgarides asked in response to the suspended sentence handed down to Eminger in the second — and likely final — NSU trial. Eminger's husband, André, had received a two-and-a-half-year prison sentence in 2018 in the first criminal trial against the terrorist group, but he was required to serve only two-thirds of it. That, too, has outraged the victims' families.

Neo-Nazi Ralf Wohlleben completed his 10-year prison sentence for aiding and abetting murder in the first NSU trial in May. This means that Beate Zschäpe remains the only person convicted in connection to the NSU who is still incarcerated; she is likely to remain behind bars until 2035. All other investigations by the Federal Prosecutor's Office against suspected NSU supporters have been dropped.
NSU documentation center planned for Nuremberg

Though legal proceedings appear to be largely concluded, the broader societal debate surrounding the unprecedented series of murders and attacks carried out by the nationalist terrorists continues. Two key projects, however, are making slow progress: the national memorial center planned for Nuremberg (Bavaria) and the memorial on Keupstraße in Cologne.

Nuremberg is an obvious choice for a national documentation center for the victims of racism and right-wing extremism. It was here where the NSU murdered its first victim, Enver Şimşek, a florist, followed by two others. Another man was badly injured here in what is believed to be the first NSU bombing.

blocks.caption: Florist Enver Şimşek was the NSU's first murder victim Image: Bernd Thissen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's more, Nuremberg also played a major role during the Nazi era. Adolf Hitler held Nazi Party rallies featuring mass marches and speeches.

The German Bundestag has been considering the idea of an NSU Documentation Center since 2024. However, plans for a swift implementation fell by the wayside because the governing coalition at the time, led by Chancellor Olaf Scholz (SPD), collapsed prematurely. The project is now set to be completed by 2030.

A response from the federal government to a parliamentary inquiry from the Greens provides initial details: Just under €9 million ($10 million) has been earmarked to create the central memorial site under the leadership of the Federal Agency for Civic Education (BpB).
Mehmet Daimagüler: "The German state protected leading neo-Nazis"
How far has Germany come in 15 years?

In Chemnitz, in the eastern German state of Saxony, a documentation center on the NSU complex has been in operation since 2025, the year in which the city was European Capital of Culture. The title of the exhibition, "Open Trial," speaks to its broad, ambitious approach as a space for education, research and events.

Gamze Kubaşık gave a speech at the opening. Her father, Mehmet, was shot and killed by the NSU in Dortmund on April 4, 2006. In fact, Chemnitz was where the terrorists Zschäpe, Mundlos and Böhnhardt had been in hiding for years. "This is also where they planned my father's murder," said Gamze Kubaşık, highlighting the significance of the location. "The support they received from the local neo-Nazi scene enabled them to carry out their schemes and reinforced their ideology."

The executive directors of the Chemnitz-based organization, Nora Krzywinski and Esther Gerstenberg, believe a national memorial and documentation center dedicated to the NSU complex is necessary. "However, it cannot replace the work being done at the actual sites of terror and to address the social conditions that gave rise to it," they emphasized in their response to a written inquiry from DW.

blocks.caption: The NSU documentation center in Chemnitz opened in 2025 Image: NSU-Dokumentationszentrum/Mark Frost

blocks.text: The guiding concept for the exhibition, Krzywinski and Gerstenberg said, is to highlight the perspectives of those affected and to link remembrance with an examination of the persistence of racism and the responsibility of the state and society. "That is why we do not view our work as a substitute for a national memorial site but rather as part of an integrated system that connects sustained local, regional and national efforts to remember and come to terms with the past in a lasting way."

Though efforts to address the multifaceted NSU complex in Chemnitz have already taken concrete form, the residents of Keupstrasse in Cologne are still waiting for the promised memorial to the 22 people injured in the June 9, 2004, nail-bomb attack. According to media reports, however, construction cannot begin until 2030 at the earliest, because old buildings around the planned site must first be demolished and new ones erected.

This means that it will take more than a quarter century until a memorial honoring the victims of the NSU bombing on Keupstrasse can be erected where it took place. Now, 15 years after the NSU was revealed, the German Bundestag has agreed to hold a debate on Thursday.
It is titled: "Commemorating the Victims, Living Up to Our Responsibilities and Taking Today's Threats Seriously."
This text was originally written in German.
